t: Autoscaling: HPA, VPA, Cluster Autoscaler, Karpenter and KEDA
sum: The control loops that size a cluster: the HPA's desired-replicas formula worked on a real metric series with tolerance, readiness handling and the five-minute scale-down window; where metrics come from; VPA's recommendations and in-place updates; node autoscaling with Cluster Autoscaler and Karpenter including consolidation; KEDA for queue-driven and scale-to-zero workloads; and the end-to-end latency of a scale-up.
prereq: sc15
Autoscaling happens at three layers — replicas, pod size and nodes — and a scale-up takes minutes because metrics, scheduling, node boot, image pull and warm-up add up.
k8s10
Requests drive scheduling and define CPU utilisation; allocatable is what nodes offer; in-place resize changes a running pod's resources.
k8s7
Deployments and StatefulSets have a replicas field that controllers reconcile; rolling updates and PodDisruptionBudgets limit disruption.
k8s6
Controllers are reconcile loops reading state through the API server; the scheduler marks pods unschedulable with FailedScheduling events.
why:
A retail API serves 3,000 requests per second at lunchtime and 200 at four in the morning. Running enough pods and nodes for lunch all day wastes most of the bill; running enough for the night collapses at noon. Autoscaling promises the obvious fix — add capacity when load rises, remove it when load falls — and Kubernetes offers it at every level: more pods, bigger pods, more nodes. Yet autoscaling is one of the most common contributors to incidents and to surprisingly high bills.

The reasons are mechanical. A team sets a CPU target, and their I/O-bound service never scales because its CPU stays at 30% while requests queue up behind a slow database. Another team's service scales up fine in the morning but takes ten minutes to scale down after a spike, and they cannot tell whether that is a bug. A batch platform wants consumers to scale to zero overnight and discovers the built-in autoscaler cannot do it. A cluster-wide autoscaler happily adds nodes for pods whose requests are three times their usage. A cost-saving node consolidator keeps restarting a fourteen-hour training job. And a flash sale peaks in forty seconds while new capacity takes four minutes to arrive.

Every one of these is predictable from the control loops involved: what signal each one reads, how often, what formula it applies, what it deliberately does slowly, and what it needs from the layers below it. sc15 introduced the three layers and why scaling takes minutes. This lesson opens each loop. It works the Horizontal Pod Autoscaler's formula on a real metric series, including the tolerance band, how it treats pods that are still starting, and the five-minute scale-down window. It follows metrics from the kubelet to the autoscaler, explains how the Vertical Pod Autoscaler learns requests and applies them, compares the two node autoscalers — Cluster Autoscaler's node groups and Karpenter's per-pod provisioning and consolidation — and shows how KEDA scales on queues and to zero. It ends with the timeline of a real scale-up and what to do about the minutes it takes.
primer:
Three thermostats in one building

Picture a building with three independent thermostats. One decides how many heaters are on in each room (the Horizontal Pod Autoscaler: how many pods). One decides how powerful each heater is (the Vertical Pod Autoscaler: how much CPU and memory each pod requests). And one decides how many rooms the building has (the node autoscaler: how many machines). Each thermostat reads its own gauge and acts on its own schedule, and none of them talks to the others. They interact only through the building: when the first thermostat switches on more heaters than the rooms can hold, the heaters wait in the corridor (pending pods), and the third thermostat, which watches the corridor, builds new rooms.

Two design choices run through all of them, and explain most of their behaviour:

  • Act on requests, not on hope. The HPA's CPU utilisation is usage divided by request; node autoscalers decide based on whether pods' requests fit. Every loop trusts requests (k8s10), so wrong requests mislead all of them.
  • Fast up, slow down. Adding capacity late hurts users; removing it early and adding it back moments later hurts both users and stability. So every loop scales up readily and scales down cautiously, with windows, thresholds and delays that look like bugs until you know why they are there.

What each loop reads, and how often

It helps to keep a one-line card for each loop. The HPA reads a metric averaged over the workload's pods every 15 seconds and writes replicas. KEDA reads an outside signal such as queue length every 30 seconds, switches a workload between zero and one replica itself, and hands the rest to an HPA. The VPA reads days of usage history and writes requests, either into new pods or into running ones. The Cluster Autoscaler reads the list of unschedulable pods every 10 seconds and writes the desired size of cloud node groups; Karpenter reads the same list and creates individual machines, and it also reads node utilisation continuously to remove or replace nodes. When an autoscaling question comes up — "why didn't it scale?" — the first step is always to ask which loop should have acted, look at the signal it reads, and check its status and events, which every one of them publishes.

Where the analogy breaks: a thermostat responds to temperature within seconds and a heater warms up in a minute. Here, the slowest step — building a new room, then moving a heater in and warming it up — takes minutes, so the autoscalers are good at following a daily curve and poor at catching a sudden spike. The building needs some spare heaters already running.
body:
1. The HPA's loop and formula

A HorizontalPodAutoscaler (API version autoscaling/v2) targets a workload's scale subresource (a Deployment, StatefulSet or anything implementing it) and lists one or more metrics with targets:

apiVersion: autoscaling/v2
kind: HorizontalPodAutoscaler
metadata: { name: api }
spec:
  scaleTargetRef: { apiVersion: apps/v1, kind: Deployment, name: api }
  minReplicas: 2
  maxReplicas: 20
  metrics:
  - type: Resource
    resource: { name: cpu, target: { type: Utilization, averageUtilization: 60 } }

The HPA controller runs inside the kube-controller-manager. Every 15 seconds (--horizontal-pod-autoscaler-sync-period) it reads the metric for the target's pods and computes:

desiredReplicas = ceil( currentReplicas × currentMetricValue / desiredMetricValue )

With a CPU utilisation target, the current value is the average over pods of usage ÷ request. Pods using 450m against a 500m request are at 90%; with a 60% target the ratio is 1.5, so 4 pods become ceil(6) = 6. Four more rules shape the result:

  1. Tolerance. If the ratio is within 0.1 of 1.0 (between 0.9 and 1.1 by default), nothing happens. This prevents constant small adjustments from noisy metrics.
  2. Multiple metrics. With several metrics, the HPA computes a desired count for each and takes the largest, so any one of them can drive a scale-up.
  3. Starting and missing pods. Pods being deleted are ignored and failed pods discarded. For CPU, pods that are not yet ready — or became ready only recently, within the initial-readiness delay (30 s) or CPU initialisation period (5 min) — and pods with no metrics are set aside. The ratio is computed from the rest, then recomputed conservatively: assume missing pods use 100% of target when the decision is a scale-down, and missing and not-ready pods use 0% when it is a scale-up. The aim is to damp decisions that are based on incomplete data, and to stop start-up CPU spikes (JIT compilation, cache warming) from triggering yet more scale-up.
  4. Behaviour. The raw recommendation passes through scaling policies and stabilization windows (section 3), and is bounded by minReplicas and maxReplicas.

The result is written to the Deployment's replicas, and the Deployment and ReplicaSet controllers do the rest (k8s7). The HPA records its reasoning in its status conditions (AbleToScale, ScalingActive, ScalingLimited) and events (SuccessfulRescale … reason: cpu resource utilization (percentage of request) above target), visible with kubectl describe hpa.

2. Where the metrics come from

The HPA reads metrics through three aggregated APIs served by add-ons, not by Kubernetes itself:

Metric typeAPIUsually served byExample
Resource (cpu, memory), ContainerResourcemetrics.k8s.iometrics-serverAverage CPU utilisation 60%
Pods, Objectcustom.metrics.k8s.ioPrometheus Adapterhttp_requests_per_second per pod = 100
Externalexternal.metrics.k8s.ioKEDA, cloud adaptersSQS queue length per pod = 20

metrics-server scrapes each kubelet's resource-metrics endpoint (which reads cgroup usage through the runtime) every 15 seconds by default and keeps only the latest values in memory. That pipeline is why the HPA's view of CPU lags reality by up to a few tens of seconds. For custom metrics, the application exports a counter such as http_requests_total to Prometheus, which scrapes it every 15-60 seconds; the adapter turns a PromQL query (rate(http_requests_total[2m]) per pod) into the custom metrics API. Each hop adds delay and averaging, which smooths noise but slows reaction. Choosing the metric is the most important decision: CPU for CPU-bound work, request rate or in-flight requests for I/O-bound services, queue depth or consumer lag for workers, and for GPU inference a serving-engine signal such as queued requests (k8s14).

3. Behaviour: why scale-down is slow on purpose

The behavior field controls the pace, separately for each direction. Without it, the defaults are:

  • Scale up: stabilization window 0 s; policies "add up to 100% of current replicas per 15 s" and "add up to 4 pods per 15 s", whichever allows more. So 2 pods can become 6 (or 4 → 8) in one step.
  • Scale down: stabilization window 300 s; policy "remove up to 100% per 15 s". The window means the HPA looks at every recommendation it made in the last five minutes and uses the highest. Capacity is only released once the need for it has been absent for five minutes.

The asymmetry is deliberate: removing pods during a brief lull and re-adding them a minute later costs a cold start each time and can turn a dip into an outage. You can tune it per HPA — a longer scale-down window for spiky services, a slower scale-up policy for services whose dependencies cannot take sudden load, or selectPolicy: Disabled to stop scale-down entirely during an event.

4. The HPA on a real metric series, worked

Take the HPA above (target 60% CPU, request 500m per pod, so the target is 300m per pod; min 2, max 20) on a service whose total CPU demand follows a lunchtime peak. Evaluate once a minute for clarity (the real loop runs every 15 s; assume demand is steady between points and new pods become ready within the minute).

t (min)Demand (m)PodsAvg utilRaw recommendationWindow (last 5 min)New replicas
01100455%ratio 0.92 → in tolerance → 4—4
11800490%ceil(4 × 1.5) = 6up: no window6
22400680%ceil(6 × 1.33) = 8up8
32600865%ratio 1.08 → tolerance → 8—8
41600840%ceil(8 × 0.67) = 6max(4,6,8,8,6) = 88
51400835%ceil(8 × 0.58) = 5max(6,8,8,6,5) = 88
61400835%5max(8,8,6,5,5) = 88
71400835%5max(8,6,5,5,5) = 88
81400835%5max(6,5,5,5,5) = 66
91400646%ceil(6 × 0.77) = 5max(5,5,5,5,5) = 55
101400556%ratio 0.93 → tolerance → 555

Read the table for three behaviours. Scale-up is immediate: at t=1 and t=2 the HPA jumps by 2 each time, well within its "double or +4 per 15 s" policy. The tolerance band absorbs small mismatches: at t=3 the pods are at 65% of target, 8% over, and nothing happens, and the same at t=10 at 7% under. Scale-down waits: from t=4 the raw recommendation falls to 6 and then 5, but the window still contains the 8s from t=2-3 until t=8, so the service carries 8 pods for four minutes longer than strictly needed. That is the cost of not flapping; whether it is the right trade depends on how fast your pods start and how spiky your traffic is.

5. The Vertical Pod Autoscaler

The HPA changes how many pods there are. The Vertical Pod Autoscaler (a separate project in the kubernetes/autoscaler repository, installed as three components) changes how big they are, by recommending and applying requests:

  • The recommender watches usage from the metrics API, keeps decaying histograms of each container's CPU and memory usage (memory based on peaks, including OOM events), and computes a target request (a high percentile plus a safety margin) with lower and upper bounds. Recommendations appear in the VPA object's status.
  • The admission controller is a mutating webhook (k8s6) that sets requests on new pods to the current recommendation.
  • The updater applies recommendations to running pods when they drift far enough, according to the updateMode: Off (recommend only), Initial (only at pod creation), Recreate (evict pods so they are recreated with new requests, respecting PodDisruptionBudgets), or InPlaceOrRecreate (use in-place resize, k8s10, falling back to eviction). The older Auto mode is deprecated in favour of the explicit ones.

VPA is best at right-sizing over days — finding that the service copied from a template with 2 CPUs and 4 GiB really needs 400m and 900 MiB — rather than reacting to a spike. Many teams run it in Off mode across the cluster and feed its recommendations into code review or a cost dashboard. The rule from the myths applies: never let HPA and VPA act on the same resource metric for the same workload.

6. Node autoscaling with Cluster Autoscaler

More replicas only help if they can be scheduled. When they cannot, they sit Pending with a FailedScheduling event, and the node autoscaler acts. The Cluster Autoscaler (CA) works with node groups — cloud groups of identical instances (an AWS Auto Scaling group, a GKE node pool) with a minimum and maximum size.

Scale-up. Every 10 seconds, CA lists unschedulable pods. For each node group it builds a template node (the instance type's allocatable resources, labels and taints) and runs the scheduler's own filtering logic in simulation: "if I added one node of this group, would these pods fit?" Several groups may qualify; an expander picks one — least-waste (least idle CPU and memory after placing the pods), priority (a configured preference order, for example spot before on-demand), random and others. CA then increases the group's desired size; the cloud launches instances, which boot, join and become Ready, and the scheduler places the pods.

Scale-down. A node becomes a candidate when the sum of its pods' requests is below 50% of its allocatable CPU and memory (--scale-down-utilization-threshold=0.5) for 10 minutes (--scale-down-unneeded-time), and every pod on it can be moved: managed by a controller, allowed by its PodDisruptionBudget, not using local storage, not annotated cluster-autoscaler.kubernetes.io/safe-to-evict: "false". CA simulates rescheduling them elsewhere, then cordons and drains the node and deletes the instance. Note "requests", not usage again: a node full of pods with inflated requests never looks underused.

The node-group model is simple and predictable, and it is also rigid: each group is one instance shape, so a cluster with varied workloads needs many groups, and a 30-CPU pod needs a group whose instances are big enough even if that is wasteful for everything else.

7. Node autoscaling with Karpenter

Karpenter (originally from AWS, now a Kubernetes SIG Autoscaling project with providers for AWS and Azure) drops node groups. A NodePool describes what nodes may be created — requirements on instance families, sizes, architectures, zones and capacity type (spot or on-demand), plus limits on total CPU and memory — and a provider-specific node class (for AWS, an EC2NodeClass) describes images, subnets and security groups.

Provisioning. Karpenter watches unschedulable pods directly, groups them by compatible constraints, and solves a bin-packing problem: which instance types, among all those the NodePool allows, can hold these pods most cheaply? Ten pending pods each requesting 1 CPU and 2 GiB might get one 16-vCPU, 32 GiB instance rather than ten small ones, or a mix that respects the pods' zone spread rules. It calls the cloud's fleet API directly, often with several instance types as options so spot capacity can be found, which usually makes nodes appear faster than a node group scale-up.

Disruption and consolidation. Karpenter also continuously removes or replaces nodes. consolidationPolicy: WhenEmptyOrUnderutilized (the default, with consolidateAfter: 0s) makes it look for nodes whose pods could run on other existing nodes (delete), or on a cheaper replacement (replace), and act on them. WhenEmpty only removes nodes with no workload pods. Nodes are also replaced when they drift from their NodePool spec (a new image) or reach an expiry age. All of this evicts pods, so it is bounded by NodePool disruption budgets (for example "at most 10% of nodes at a time", or none during a schedule), by PodDisruptionBudgets, and by the karpenter.sh/do-not-disrupt annotation on pods that must finish, such as long training runs. Spot interruption notices are handled by draining the node before the cloud reclaims it.

Cluster AutoscalerKarpenter
Unit of scalingNode groups of one shapeIndividual nodes of any allowed shape
DecisionSimulate on group templates, expander picksBin-pack pending pods across instance types
Scale-downRequests < 50% for 10 min, pods movableContinuous consolidation (delete or replace)
Cost focusVia expanders and group designBuilt in (cheapest fit, spot, consolidation)
Disruption controlPDBs, annotations, timingsDisruption budgets, PDBs, do-not-disrupt

8. KEDA: events, queues and zero

Some workloads should scale on something outside the cluster: messages waiting in a queue, lag on a Kafka topic, rows in a table, a schedule. And some should scale to zero when there is nothing to do. KEDA (Kubernetes Event-Driven Autoscaling, a CNCF graduated project) provides both. A ScaledObject names a workload and one or more triggers from KEDA's catalogue of scalers:

apiVersion: keda.sh/v1alpha1
kind: ScaledObject
metadata: { name: thumbnailer }
spec:
  scaleTargetRef: { name: thumbnailer }
  minReplicaCount: 0          # scale to zero
  maxReplicaCount: 50
  pollingInterval: 30         # default 30 s
  cooldownPeriod: 300         # default 300 s before returning to zero
  triggers:
  - type: aws-sqs-queue
    metadata: { queueURL: https://sqs.us-east-1.amazonaws.com/123456789012/thumbs,
                queueLength: "20", activationQueueLength: "1", awsRegion: us-east-1 }

KEDA splits the job. Its operator polls the trigger every pollingInterval and handles the 0↔1 transitions itself: when the queue exceeds the activation threshold (here one message) it scales the Deployment from 0 to 1; when the trigger has been inactive for cooldownPeriod, it scales back to 0. For 1↔N it creates and manages an ordinary HPA whose metric is an external metric served by KEDA's metrics server, with a per-replica target — here 20 messages per replica. With 340 messages queued, the HPA computes ceil(340 / 20) = 17 replicas (the ratio form of the same formula). As workers drain the queue, the HPA's scale-down window brings replicas down, and when the queue has been empty for five minutes, KEDA takes it to zero.

For work that should run as discrete batches, a ScaledJob creates Jobs (k8s7) in proportion to pending events instead of scaling long-running consumers, which suits long tasks that should not be interrupted by a scale-down. Scale-to-zero always buys cost with latency: the first message after a quiet period waits for a pod to be scheduled, pulled and started — seconds for a small image on a warm node, minutes for a GPU model on a new one.

9. The end-to-end timeline of a scale-up

Put the layers together for a surge on a cluster with no spare nodes:

Roughly: 15-60 s for the metric to reflect the surge; up to 15 s for the HPA; seconds for the scheduler and node autoscaler to react; 60-120 s for an instance to boot, run its bootstrap, register and become Ready (network plugin up); seconds to minutes to pull the image; then the application's start and warm-up before readiness passes. Two to five minutes is normal. If the surge peaks in 30 seconds, all of it arrives too late.

The practical answers are layered. Headroom: target 50-70% utilisation, not 90%, so existing pods absorb a burst. Overprovisioning: run a Deployment of low-priority placeholder pods (a pause image with real requests and a negative-priority PriorityClass); real pods preempt them instantly (k8s10), and the evicted placeholders become pending, which makes the node autoscaler add a node in the background. Scheduled scaling for known events (raise minReplicas before the sale, with a CronJob or KEDA's cron trigger). Faster start: small images (k8s3), pre-pulled images on node images, lazy-loading snapshotters, fast application start. And load shedding for what nobody predicted (sc12).

10. Choosing and testing an autoscaling setup

Choosing comes down to three questions. What signal tracks the load this workload's users feel? CPU for CPU-bound request handling; request rate or concurrency for I/O-bound services; queue depth or lag for consumers; serving-engine queues for model inference. That picks the HPA metric or the KEDA trigger. How fast must capacity follow, and how fast can it arrive? If new pods take ten seconds and the traffic curve is daily, reactive scaling is enough; if pods take minutes or traffic jumps in seconds, add headroom, overprovisioning or scheduled scaling. What should the nodes look like? A few uniform workloads fit node groups and the Cluster Autoscaler; varied workloads, spot capacity and cost pressure favour Karpenter, with disruption budgets set before it is enabled. VPA sits beside all of these in recommendation mode, keeping requests honest.

Testing matters because autoscaling only acts under load, which is exactly when you cannot afford to discover it misbehaves. A useful drill: run a load test that ramps traffic from baseline to twice the expected peak over ten minutes, holds, then drops sharply. Record replica count, pending pods, node count and the latency percentiles against time. You should see replicas follow the ramp within a minute or two, pending pods appear briefly as nodes are added, latency stay within its objective during the ramp (if it does not, headroom is too low or start-up too slow), and capacity hold for the scale-down window after the drop before shrinking without errors. Repeat after any change to the metric, the requests, the images or the node configuration.
deep:
Why the HPA is a proportional controller, and what that implies

The HPA's formula makes the replica count proportional to the ratio of observed to target metric: a pure proportional controller, with a dead band (the tolerance) and asymmetric rate limits. It assumes the metric per pod falls in proportion as pods are added — true for CPU on a load-balanced stateless service, false when the bottleneck is elsewhere. If a database is saturated, adding API pods raises neither throughput nor lowers per-pod latency; a latency-based HPA will keep scaling up against maxReplicas and make the database worse. Good HPA metrics are ones the pods themselves control; when they are not, cap maxReplicas at what downstream systems can take and alert when the HPA sits at its maximum.

Metric staleness and the feedback delay

A control loop with a delay between action and observed effect overshoots. Here the delay is long: new pods take a minute or more to start contributing, and CPU metrics are averages over scrape windows. The HPA compensates by ignoring not-yet-ready pods' CPU and by the scale-down window, but scale-up can still overshoot when a burst is short: the HPA sees 150% utilisation, doubles, and by the time the new pods are ready the burst is over. That overshoot is usually acceptable (capacity is released five minutes later); undershoot during sustained growth is not. Scaling on a leading indicator such as request rate or queue depth rather than a lagging one such as CPU reduces both.

Bin packing, fragmentation and why node autoscalers disagree with intuition

A cluster at 40% average utilisation can still have pending pods if the free capacity is scattered in pieces too small for them — 1.5 CPUs free on each of ten nodes cannot hold one 2-CPU pod. Node autoscalers fix that by adding a node, raising cost while utilisation falls further. Consolidation (Karpenter) or descheduling (k8s10) reverses fragmentation by moving pods so whole nodes empty out, at the price of disruption. Requests, again, sit underneath: pods with 2-CPU requests and 300m usage fragment a cluster that would otherwise pack easily, which is why right-sizing with VPA recommendations often saves more than any autoscaler setting.

Spot capacity and interruption

Spot or preemptible instances cost a fraction of on-demand but can be reclaimed with a short notice (two minutes on AWS). Node autoscalers make them practical: Karpenter and CA's priority expander prefer spot pools, diversify across many instance types so a shortage in one does not block scaling, and fall back to on-demand. Interruption handling turns the cloud's notice into a cordon and drain so pods move gracefully. Workloads still need to tolerate it: stateless services with several replicas spread across nodes, PodDisruptionBudgets, and checkpointing for batch and training jobs. Keeping a baseline of on-demand capacity for the minimum replicas, and running bursts on spot, is the usual compromise.

Predictive and scheduled scaling

Reactive loops can only follow; for traffic with strong daily or weekly patterns, the lag can be removed by acting on a forecast. The simplest form is scheduled scaling: raise minReplicas (or a KEDA cron trigger's desired count) half an hour before the morning ramp and lower it in the evening, letting the HPA handle deviations. More elaborate systems fit a forecast to past traffic and set the floor from it. Both keep the reactive HPA as the safety net and simply move the starting point, so a forecast error costs some money rather than an outage.

Autoscaling stateful and GPU workloads

Scaling a StatefulSet's replicas is mechanically identical, but adding a database replica or a Kafka broker means data movement that takes far longer than pod start-up, so these are scaled by operators or humans on capacity plans rather than by an HPA reacting to minutes of load. GPU inference sits in between: replicas are stateless, but each holds a model that takes tens of seconds to minutes to load, and nodes are scarce and slow to provision. The patterns that work are leading metrics from the serving engine (queue length, KV-cache use), conservative scale-down, warm pools of nodes or placeholder pods, and caching model weights on nodes so a new replica on a warm node starts in seconds (k8s14).

Cost as a feedback signal

Autoscalers optimise what they can see — metrics and pending pods — not money. Closing the loop on cost means feeding it back: per-namespace cost from requests multiplied by node prices (tools such as OpenCost do this), alerts when a workload's requested-to-used ratio drifts upward, and reviews of HPA minimums, which quietly set the floor of a service's spend. A service whose HPA never drops below its minimum is not autoscaled at all; it is a fixed fleet with extra steps.
prod:
The case: the HPA algorithm and Karpenter's consolidation, as documented

The Kubernetes documentation's "algorithm details" section is the authoritative account of the behaviours that most often confuse teams in production, and reading it explains a long list of tickets. It states the formula and the 0.1 default tolerance; that pods with a deletion timestamp are ignored and failed pods discarded; that for CPU, pods not yet ready — judged with a 30-second initial-readiness delay and a five-minute CPU initialisation period — and pods with missing metrics are set aside; and that the average is then recomputed "more conservatively, assuming those pods were consuming 100% of the desired value in case of a scale down, and 0% in case of a scale up". It also documents that with multiple metrics the largest recommendation wins, and the default behaviour: no stabilization for scale-up with doubling-or-four-pods policies, and a 300-second window for scale-down. Teams who see "the HPA didn't scale even though CPU was high" usually find not-ready pods dampening the decision or the tolerance band; teams who see "it took five minutes to scale down" have met the window.

Karpenter's disruption documentation plays the same role for node churn. It states that if not set, NodePools use consolidationPolicy: WhenEmptyOrUnderutilized with consolidateAfter: 0s — the most aggressive cost setting — and explains the trade-off: WhenEmpty for the most conservative behaviour, underutilised consolidation for savings at the cost of moving pods. Teams adopting Karpenter for its fast provisioning are often surprised by regular pod evictions on day two; the documented remedies are disruption budgets on the NodePool, PodDisruptionBudgets on workloads, a longer consolidateAfter, and karpenter.sh/do-not-disrupt on pods that must not move.

Failure modes and symptoms

  • HPA shows <unknown> targets: metrics-server or the adapter is down, or pods have no requests for the resource. Events say FailedGetResourceMetric.
  • Never scales despite load: wrong metric (CPU on an I/O-bound service), requests too high, or pinned at maxReplicas (condition ScalingLimited).
  • Flapping: a too-short scale-down window, or HPA and VPA fighting.
  • Pods pending, no new nodes: node group at its maximum, no instance type satisfies the pods' constraints, cloud capacity or quota exhausted, or a taint and toleration mismatch the autoscaler's template does not satisfy; CA and Karpenter both log why.
  • Nodes never scale down: pods without controllers, local storage, restrictive PDBs (maxUnavailable: 0), safe-to-evict: false, or system pods without PDBs on every node.
  • Regular unexplained evictions: consolidation, spot interruptions or node expiry.
  • Autoscaling made it worse: scaling out a service whose bottleneck is downstream overloads the dependency; cap replicas and shed load.

Knobs, in order of impact

The metric and its target; accurate requests; minReplicas (your floor of headroom); the scale-down stabilization window; scale-up policies for dependencies that cannot take sudden load; node autoscaler limits and instance diversity; consolidation policy and disruption budgets; and the size of the overprovisioning buffer.

What to watch

HPA current versus desired replicas and time at max; the HPA's metric versus target; pending pod count and age; time from pod creation to Ready on new nodes (the scale-up latency you actually have); node count and cost by capacity type; consolidation and interruption events; and the ratio of requested to used CPU and memory across the cluster, which bounds how much any autoscaler can save.

A note on limits

Every autoscaler should have a ceiling that reflects what the rest of the system can absorb: maxReplicas sized to downstream capacity and connection limits, NodePool or node-group limits sized to budget and cloud quotas. Hitting a ceiling should page someone, because it means demand exceeded what was planned for, and the answer is a decision, not an automatic scale-up.
myths: The HPA scales on how busy the pods are.

The CPU-utilisation HPA scales on usage divided by request. If requests are wrong, utilisation is wrong: a service with a 2-CPU request using 0.5 CPU looks 25% utilised however overloaded it really is, and a service with no CPU request cannot be autoscaled on CPU at all.
Autoscaling handles traffic spikes.

Each layer reacts in seconds to minutes: metrics are scraped every 15-60 seconds, the HPA evaluates every 15 seconds, new nodes take one to several minutes, and images and application warm-up add more. A spike that peaks in seconds is over before capacity arrives. Headroom, pre-scaling and load shedding handle spikes; autoscaling handles curves.
Running HPA and VPA together is fine.

If both act on CPU, they fight: VPA raises requests, which lowers utilisation, which makes the HPA scale in, which raises per-pod usage, which makes VPA raise requests again. Use them on different signals (HPA on requests per second or a custom metric, VPA on CPU and memory), or use VPA in recommendation-only mode.
Scale to zero is just minReplicas: 0.

The built-in HPA cannot scale to zero by default, because with zero pods there is no per-pod metric to compute a ratio from. Scale to zero needs an external signal that exists without pods — queue length, request count at a proxy — and something that scales 0 to 1, such as KEDA or Knative, plus tolerance for the cold start.
Cluster Autoscaler adds nodes when nodes are busy.

It adds nodes when pods are unschedulable, that is when their requests do not fit anywhere. High CPU usage on existing nodes triggers nothing. Likewise it removes nodes when their requested resources are low and their pods can be placed elsewhere, not when they are idle by usage.
Karpenter is just a faster Cluster Autoscaler.

Karpenter does not scale predefined node groups. It looks at pending pods' requirements and launches whatever instance types and sizes fit them best from a NodePool's allowed set, and it continuously consolidates — replacing or removing nodes to cut cost — which disrupts pods by design and must be bounded with disruption budgets and PodDisruptionBudgets.
lab:
Steps 1-2 need a kind or minikube cluster with metrics-server (on minikube: minikube addons enable metrics-server; on kind, install metrics-server with --kubelet-insecure-tls). Step 3 runs here with Python 3.12.

  1. Watch an HPA react (Needs a kind/minikube cluster). Following the Kubernetes HPA walkthrough: 
    kubectl apply -f https://k8s.io/examples/application/php-apache.yaml
kubectl autoscale deployment php-apache --cpu-percent=50 --min=1 --max=10
kubectl run -i --tty load-generator --rm --image=busybox:1.37 --restart=Never -- \
  /bin/sh -c "while sleep 0.01; do wget -q -O- http://php-apache; done"
kubectl get hpa php-apache --watch
    The docs show TARGETS rising to a few hundred percent (e.g. cpu: 305%/50%) and REPLICAS climbing within a minute or two. Stop the load generator and keep watching: replicas stay up for about five minutes (the scale-down window) before dropping back to 1.
  2. Read the reasoning (Needs a cluster). kubectl describe hpa php-apache: conditions and events such as New size: 4; reason: cpu resource utilization (percentage of request) above target. Then add a behavior.scaleDown.stabilizationWindowSeconds: 60 and repeat: scale-down now happens after a minute.
  3. Simulate the HPA on a series (runs here). Save as hpasim.py: 
    import math
def hpa(demand_m, request_m=500, target=60, start=4, lo=2, hi=20, tol=0.1, window=5):
    pods, recs = start, []
    for t, d in enumerate(demand_m):
        util = d * 100 // (pods * request_m)      # integer percent, as the HPA computes it
        ratio = util / target
        rec = pods if abs(1 - ratio) <= tol else math.ceil(pods * ratio)
        rec = max(lo, min(hi, rec, max(pods * 2, pods + 4)))   # scale-up policy
        recs.append(rec)
        new = rec if rec >= pods else max(recs[-window:])       # scale-down window
        print(f"t={t:2} demand={d:5} pods={pods:2} util={util:3}% rec={rec:2} -> {new}")
        pods = new
demand = [1100, 1800, 2400, 2600, 1600, 1400, 1400, 1400, 1400, 1400, 1400]
hpa(demand)
print("--- KEDA-style queue target 20 per replica:")
for q in (0, 1, 45, 340, 120, 0):
    print(q, "messages ->", 0 if q == 0 else math.ceil(q / 20), "replicas")
    Expect the table from body section 4: 4, 6, 8, 8, then 8 held until t=8, then 6, 5. Change window=1 to see immediate scale-down, and tol=0 to see small adjustments every minute.
recap: The HPA computes desiredReplicas = ceil(currentReplicas × currentMetric / targetMetric) every 15 seconds, skips changes when the ratio is within 10% of 1, and takes the maximum across metrics when several are configured.
For CPU it sets aside pods that are not yet ready or lack metrics and recomputes conservatively, assuming 0% usage for them when scaling up and 100% when scaling down.
Scale-up is immediate by default (up to doubling or +4 pods per 15 seconds); scale-down uses the highest recommendation of the last 300 seconds, so capacity is released slowly.
Resource metrics come from metrics-server; custom and external metrics come through an adapter such as Prometheus Adapter or KEDA's metrics server.

VPA's recommender learns usage distributions and sets target requests; its updater applies them by eviction or, with InPlaceOrRecreate, by in-place resize; HPA and VPA must not both act on the same metric.
Cluster Autoscaler adds nodes to node groups when pods are unschedulable and removes nodes whose requested utilisation is below 50% for 10 minutes when their pods can move.
Karpenter provisions individual nodes sized to pending pods from flexible instance requirements and consolidates underused nodes, governed by NodePool disruption settings.
KEDA scales on event sources such as queues and streams, handles 0↔1 itself and feeds an HPA for 1↔N, with a 30-second polling interval and 300-second cooldown by default.
A full scale-up from metric change to a ready pod on a new node commonly takes two to five minutes, so autoscaling is paired with headroom, overprovisioning and fast start-up.
glossary: activation threshold
In KEDA, the metric value above which a workload scaled to zero is activated to one replica.
Cluster Autoscaler
A Kubernetes project that resizes cloud node groups: adds nodes when pods cannot be scheduled, removes underused nodes.
consolidation
Karpenter's process of removing or replacing nodes so the same pods run on fewer or cheaper nodes.
cooldownPeriod
In KEDA, how long to wait after the last active trigger before scaling a workload back to zero (300 s by default).
custom metrics API
An aggregated Kubernetes API (custom.metrics.k8s.io) through which an adapter serves per-object metrics such as requests per second to the HPA.
external metrics API
An aggregated API (external.metrics.k8s.io) serving metrics not tied to Kubernetes objects, such as queue length.
HorizontalPodAutoscaler (HPA)
A controller that adjusts a workload's replica count to keep a metric near a target.
Karpenter
A node autoscaler that launches right-sized nodes directly for pending pods and consolidates underused capacity.
KEDA
Kubernetes Event-Driven Autoscaling: scales workloads on external event sources, including to and from zero.
metrics-server
A cluster add-on that collects CPU and memory usage from kubelets and serves it through the resource metrics API.
node group
A set of identical nodes managed as one scaling unit by a cloud (an Auto Scaling group or managed node pool).
NodePool (Karpenter)
A Karpenter object describing which nodes may be created (instance types, zones, capacity type), limits, and disruption policy.
overprovisioning
Keeping spare capacity with low-priority placeholder pods that real pods can preempt instantly.
ScaledObject
A KEDA object that links a workload to triggers (event sources) and scaling parameters.
stabilization window
A period over which the HPA considers past recommendations, using the highest (for scale-down) or lowest (for scale-up) to avoid flapping.
tolerance
The fraction by which the metric ratio may differ from 1 before the HPA acts (0.1 by default).
VerticalPodAutoscaler (VPA)
A project that recommends and optionally applies CPU and memory requests based on observed usage.
drill:
Design: autoscaling a queue-driven document pipeline

A document-processing service pulls jobs from an SQS queue. Each job takes 20-40 seconds of CPU on one core; each worker pod (request 1 CPU, 1 GiB) processes one job at a time. Traffic: near zero overnight, 2,000 jobs per hour on weekdays, and month-end bursts of 30,000 jobs within an hour. The business wants jobs finished within 15 minutes of arrival and the lowest cost overnight. Today the Deployment has a CPU-based HPA (target 70%, min 3, max 30) and a fixed node group of 10 four-core nodes. Diagnose the current setup and design a better one.

Answer

Current problems: CPU utilisation saturates at ~100% for any busy worker whether one job or a thousand are queued, so the HPA cannot tell a backlog from steady load and scales to at most a ratio of 100/70 per step; minimum 3 wastes capacity overnight; and 10 nodes cap the cluster at about 36 workers (after DaemonSets), far below month-end needs.

Sizing: at 30 s average, a worker handles about 120 jobs per hour. Weekday load of 2,000 per hour needs ~17 workers. A 30,000-job burst finished within roughly 15 minutes of arrival means draining ~30,000 jobs in about an hour plus the 15-minute target: around 250-300 workers at peak (30,000 ÷ 120 ≈ 250 worker-hours).

Design: a KEDA ScaledObject on the SQS queue with a per-replica target of about 10 queued messages (so the backlog per worker stays under ~5 minutes), minReplicaCount: 0, activation at 1 message, maxReplicaCount: 300, a scale-up policy allowing large jumps, and a scale-down window of several minutes. Karpenter (or CA with a large node group and the least-waste expander) for nodes, preferring spot with on-demand fallback and many instance types; workers must handle SIGTERM by finishing or returning the current job to the queue (visibility timeout) so spot interruptions and scale-down lose nothing. Overnight, the first job waits for a cold start — acceptable against a 15-minute target. For month-end, add a scheduled pre-scale (KEDA cron trigger) shortly before the known burst, so nodes are ready when it arrives. Monitor queue age (the SLO metric), not just length.
qa: E
What does the HPA do and how often?

It adjusts a workload's replicas so that a metric stays near a target. Every 15 seconds by default it reads the metric, computes desired = ceil(current replicas × current value / target value), bounds it by minReplicas and maxReplicas and its scaling policies, and writes the result to the workload's scale subresource. It does nothing if the ratio is within 10% of 1.
E
What are the three layers of autoscaling?

Replicas (HPA, KEDA) change how many pods run; pod size (VPA, in-place resize) changes each pod's requests; nodes (Cluster Autoscaler, Karpenter) change how many machines the cluster has. They are separate loops: more replicas only help if nodes have room, and node autoscalers react to the pending pods that replica scaling creates.
E
Why does the HPA need resource requests?

CPU and memory utilisation targets are percentages of the request. Without a request, utilisation is undefined and the HPA reports the metric as unknown and does not scale. With an inaccurate request, utilisation misstates load, so scaling happens too late or too early.
M
Compute the HPA's decision: 8 pods, target 60% CPU, current average 40%.

desired = ceil(8 × 40 / 60) = ceil(5.33) = 6. But scale-down uses a 300-second stabilization window: the HPA takes the highest recommendation from the last five minutes. If a minute ago it recommended 8, it keeps 8 until that recommendation ages out, then drops to the highest remaining one.
Follow-up: And at 65%? — 65/60 = 1.083, within the 10% tolerance, so no change.
M
How does the HPA treat new pods that aren't ready yet?

For CPU, pods that are not yet ready, or whose latest sample predates readiness, are set aside, as are pods missing metrics. The ratio is computed from the rest, then recomputed conservatively: when scaling up, missing and not-ready pods are assumed to use 0% of the target; when scaling down, missing ones are assumed to use 100%. This prevents start-up CPU spikes from triggering more scale-up and prevents missing data from causing scale-down.
M
When would you scale on something other than CPU?

When CPU doesn't track load: I/O-bound services waiting on databases or APIs (scale on requests per second or concurrency), queue consumers (scale on queue depth or consumer lag), GPU inference (scale on queue depth, batch occupancy or GPU utilisation), latency-sensitive services where tail latency rises before CPU does. Expose the metric through Prometheus Adapter or KEDA and target a per-pod value.
M
How does Cluster Autoscaler decide to add or remove nodes?

Every 10 seconds it looks for unschedulable pods, simulates scheduling them on a template node of each node group, and asks an expander (least-waste, priority, random…) to pick a group to grow. For scale-down, a node whose requested CPU and memory are below 50% of allocatable for 10 minutes is a candidate if all its pods can be rescheduled elsewhere, respecting PodDisruptionBudgets and annotations that block eviction; then it drains and deletes it.
M
What does KEDA add to the HPA?

Scalers for dozens of event sources — Kafka lag, SQS and RabbitMQ queue length, Prometheus queries, cron schedules — exposed as external metrics to an HPA it manages, and scaling to and from zero, which the HPA cannot do: KEDA's operator activates the workload from 0 to 1 when the trigger crosses its activation threshold and deactivates it after the cooldown period. ScaledJobs create Jobs per batch of events instead of scaling a Deployment.
H
Trace the time from a traffic surge to new capacity serving, on a full cluster.

Metrics lag: the app's usage rises, metrics-server or Prometheus picks it up within 15-60 s. The HPA evaluates every 15 s and scales the Deployment. New pods are Pending because nodes are full; the node autoscaler notices within about 10 s, launches instances, and the node boots, joins and becomes Ready in typically 60-120 s. Then the kubelet pulls the image (seconds to minutes) and the app starts and warms up until readiness passes. Two to five minutes in total is common, which is why latency-critical services keep headroom or low-priority placeholder pods.
Follow-up: Which step would you attack first for a 10 GB inference image? — The image pull: pre-pull on node images, lazy-loading snapshotters, or a node-local model cache, then the node boot time.
H
HPA and VPA fight over a service. Explain the loop and the fix.

VPA observes high CPU usage relative to requests and raises the request; utilisation (usage / request) drops, so the HPA scales in; the remaining pods each carry more load, usage per pod rises, and VPA raises requests further, or the reverse oscillation. The fix is to give each a different signal: HPA on requests per second, queue depth or a custom metric, VPA on CPU and memory sizing; or use VPA in Off mode for recommendations only and apply them in reviews.
H
Karpenter consolidation keeps restarting your pods. What is happening, and how do you control it?

With consolidationPolicy WhenEmptyOrUnderutilized and consolidateAfter 0s (the defaults), Karpenter continuously looks for nodes it can delete or replace with cheaper ones and moves their pods, so workloads see regular evictions. Control it with NodePool disruption budgets (for example at most 10% of nodes at once, or none during business hours), a longer consolidateAfter, PodDisruptionBudgets on the workloads, and the karpenter.sh/do-not-disrupt annotation on pods that must not be interrupted, such as long training jobs.
Follow-up: Why not just use WhenEmpty? — It is safer but leaves underused nodes running, so cost savings shrink; it is a dial between cost and disruption.
H
Design autoscaling for an LLM inference service on GPUs with a strict p95 latency SLO.

Scale replicas on a signal that leads latency: requests in queue or in flight per replica, or batch occupancy from the serving engine, through KEDA or Prometheus Adapter, not CPU and usually not raw GPU utilisation. Keep minReplicas above zero for the SLO, and use scale-to-zero only for low-priority models. Scale nodes with Karpenter or node groups per GPU type, with overprovisioning placeholders, because a GPU node plus a multi-gigabyte model can take several minutes to become ready. Use a long scale-down stabilization window, and cache model weights on nodes to cut cold starts (k8s14).

Scale-up simulation, expanders, scale-down conditions and overprovisioning.
Recommender, updater and admission controller; update modes including InPlaceOrRecreate.
Consolidation policies, consolidateAfter, drift, expiry and disruption budgets.
Triggers, pollingInterval (30 s), cooldownPeriod (300 s), min/max replicas and fallback.
metrics-server and the resource metrics API used by the HPA and kubectl top.

t: Packaging and delivery: Helm, Kustomize and GitOps with Argo CD or Flux
sum: How teams stop copy-pasting YAML: a Helm chart rendered by hand (values precedence, helpers, whitespace, checksums), how Helm stores and rolls back releases and what changed in Helm 4, Kustomize bases, overlays and generators, and GitOps — Argo CD and Flux reconciling a cluster from Git, promotion and rollback by commit — with the Argo CD Helm path-traversal advisory as the case.
prereq: k8s6
kubectl apply sends objects to the API server; server-side apply tracks which manager owns which fields; controllers reconcile desired with actual state.
k8s7
Deployments roll out a new ReplicaSet whenever the pod template changes and keep old ones for rollback.
k8s9
ConfigMaps and Secrets hold configuration; changing a ConfigMap does not restart pods that read it as environment variables.
swe9
Build once and promote the same artefact; rolling, blue-green and canary releases; rollback and roll forward.
sc15
Infrastructure as code and GitOps keep desired state in Git, applied by an agent that also reverts drift.
why:
A team's first Kubernetes service is five YAML files applied with kubectl apply -f from a laptop. Six months later they run twelve services in three environments. Each service has a Deployment, a Service, a ConfigMap, an HPA, a PodDisruptionBudget, an HTTPRoute and a ServiceAccount, and each environment needs slightly different replicas, resources, hostnames and image tags. Someone copies the staging directory to make production and edits it by hand. A fix to the readiness probe is made in staging and forgotten in production. A colleague scales a Deployment with kubectl scale during an incident and nobody remembers to put it back. A deploy is run from a laptop with an uncommitted change. Nobody can say for certain what is running in production or who changed it.

Three families of tools address this, at different levels. Helm turns manifests into parameterised templates packaged as versioned charts, installs them as releases with history and rollback, and is how most third-party software (databases, ingress controllers, monitoring stacks) is distributed. Kustomize, built into kubectl, keeps one plain set of manifests and applies declared patches to produce each environment's variant, without any templating. And GitOps — with agents such as Argo CD and Flux — changes who applies the manifests: instead of people or CI pushing to the cluster, an agent in the cluster pulls the desired state from Git, applies it, and keeps putting it back whenever the cluster drifts.

Each brings its own mechanics and its own sharp edges: template whitespace that silently produces wrong YAML; a rollback that does not roll back a database; config changes that never restart pods; an autoscaler and a GitOps agent fighting over the same field; and the uncomfortable fact that the components rendering your manifests can read a great deal. In 2022 a vulnerability in Argo CD's Helm rendering let any user who could create an Application read files outside their repository, including other applications' decrypted secrets.

This lesson renders a Helm chart by hand, line by line, follows a release through upgrade and rollback and what Helm 4 changed, builds Kustomize overlays, and then sets up the GitOps loop with Argo CD and Flux, including promotion, rollback, secrets and the failure modes that matter in production.
primer:
Forms, tracing paper and a librarian

Three analogies, one per tool. Helm is a form with blanks. The chart's templates are a standard contract with blanks for the name, the number of copies, the image; the values file fills the blanks; the result is a completed contract (a manifest) that Kubernetes understands. Helm also keeps a filed copy of every contract it has submitted for each installation, so it can resubmit an older one to undo a change.

Kustomize is tracing paper. You keep one clean drawing (the base: complete, valid manifests). For production you lay a sheet of tracing paper over it and draw only the differences — more replicas here, a bigger memory limit there, a different image tag. The final picture is the base with the overlay on top. Nothing in the base has blanks; you can read it as it is.

GitOps is a librarian with a catalogue. The catalogue (Git) says exactly which books should be on which shelves. The librarian (Argo CD or Flux) walks the shelves continuously, puts back anything missing, removes anything that should not be there, and re-shelves books that someone moved. If you want a change, you change the catalogue — through review — and the librarian makes the shelves match.

Why not just a script?

Before adopting any of this, teams often write a shell script that substitutes variables into YAML with sed or envsubst and pipes the result to kubectl apply. It works for a while, and its failure modes explain what the real tools add. A script has no memory of what it applied last time, so a resource removed from the files is never deleted from the cluster (Helm releases and GitOps pruning track that). It has no idea about Kubernetes structure, so replacing a value inside a list or merging two maps becomes fragile string manipulation (Kustomize's strategic merge and Helm's values merging understand the shapes). It cannot roll back to "what was running before" without someone reconstructing the inputs (Helm revisions and Git history record them). And it runs wherever it is run from, with whatever credentials that place has, so the cluster's state depends on whose laptop last ran it (GitOps moves the applying into the cluster). Each tool in this lesson is, in part, the hard-won answer to one of those problems.

The tools compose. Helm and Kustomize decide what the manifests are; GitOps decides how and when they reach the cluster. Argo CD and Flux both render Helm charts and Kustomize overlays as part of their loop.

Where the analogies break: a form, a tracing and a catalogue all describe the cluster's objects, not its data. Re-submitting an old contract, reverting an overlay or rolling back a catalogue entry restores manifests; it does not restore a database schema that the newer version migrated, or files a job wrote. Delivery tools manage desired state; data needs its own plan (swe9's expand-contract migrations, k8s9's snapshots and backups).
body:
1. What packaging has to do

Look at what differs between environments for one service and what stays the same. The same: the container port, probes, labels and selectors, the Service, the security context, the shape of the HPA. Different: the image tag (dev runs today's build, production last week's), replicas and resources, hostnames on the HTTPRoute, a few configuration values, sometimes extra objects (a PodDisruptionBudget only in production). A packaging tool must let you express "the same, except…" without copying, make the result reviewable as ordinary manifests, and, ideally, make config changes roll pods. Helm and Kustomize take opposite approaches to the "except".

2. A Helm chart's anatomy

web/
  Chart.yaml          # apiVersion: v2, name: web, version: 1.4.0 (chart), appVersion: "2.7.1" (app)
  values.yaml         # defaults
  values.schema.json  # optional JSON Schema for values
  templates/
    _helpers.tpl      # named templates (not rendered on their own)
    deployment.yaml
    service.yaml
    configmap.yaml
    hpa.yaml
    NOTES.txt         # printed after install
  charts/             # dependencies (subcharts), declared in Chart.yaml

The chart's version is the package's version; appVersion is the version of the software inside, often used as the default image tag. Charts are distributed as .tgz archives in HTTP chart repositories or, increasingly, as OCI artefacts in the same registries as images (helm push web-1.4.0.tgz oci://ghcr.io/myorg/charts), where they can be signed like images (k8s5).

3. Rendering a template by hand

Templates use Go's text/template language extended with the Sprig function library. Here are the relevant pieces of the chart:

# values.yaml
replicaCount: 2
image:
  repository: ghcr.io/myorg/web
  tag: ""               # empty: fall back to appVersion
resources:
  requests: { cpu: 250m, memory: 256Mi }
config:
  LOG_LEVEL: info

# templates/_helpers.tpl
{{- define "web.fullname" -}}
{{- printf "%s-%s" .Release.Name .Chart.Name | trunc 63 | trimSuffix "-" -}}
{{- end -}}
{{- define "web.labels" -}}
app.kubernetes.io/name: {{ .Chart.Name }}
app.kubernetes.io/instance: {{ .Release.Name }}
{{- end -}}

# templates/deployment.yaml
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: {{ include "web.fullname" . }}
  labels:
    {{- include "web.labels" . | nindent 4 }}
spec:
  replicas: {{ .Values.replicaCount }}
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      {{- include "web.labels" . | nindent 6 }}
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        {{- include "web.labels" . | nindent 8 }}
      annotations:
        checksum/config: {{ include (print $.Template.BasePath "/configmap.yaml") . | sha256sum }}
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: web
        image: "{{ .Values.image.repository }}:{{ .Values.image.tag | default .Chart.AppVersion }}"
        {{- with .Values.resources }}
        resources:
          {{- toYaml . | nindent 10 }}
        {{- end }}

Now install it for production:

helm upgrade --install shop ./web -n prod -f values-prod.yaml --set image.tag=2.7.2

with values-prod.yaml containing replicaCount: 6 and resources: {requests: {cpu: "1", memory: 1Gi}, limits: {memory: 1Gi}}. Render it step by step.

  1. Merge values, later sources overriding earlier ones: the chart's values.yaml, then each -f file in order, then --set. Maps are merged key by key; lists and scalars are replaced. Result: replicaCount: 6; image.repository: ghcr.io/myorg/web (from defaults), image.tag: 2.7.2 (from --set); resources is a map, so it is merged: requests from the prod file replaces the default requests map key by key (cpu: "1", memory: 1Gi), and limits is added; config.LOG_LEVEL: info from defaults.
  2. Build the context (the "dot"): .Values (merged values), .Release (Name: shop, Namespace: prod, Revision, IsUpgrade), .Chart (from Chart.yaml), .Capabilities (the cluster's Kubernetes version and APIs) and .Template.
  3. {{ include "web.fullname" . }} runs the named template with the same context: printf "%s-%s" gives shop-web; trunc 63 keeps it within the 63-character limit for names; trimSuffix "-" removes a trailing dash that truncation might leave. Output: shop-web.
  4. Whitespace. {{- trims all whitespace (including the newline) to its left, -}} to its right. In labels: followed by {{- include "web.labels" . | nindent 4 }}, the {{- eats the newline after labels:; nindent 4 then adds a newline and indents every line of the helper's output by four spaces. Result: the two label lines appear correctly nested under labels:. Using indent instead of nindent, or forgetting the dash, produces lines at the wrong depth — sometimes invalid YAML, sometimes valid YAML with the labels attached to the wrong key, which is worse.
  5. {{ .Values.replicaCount }} prints 6.
  6. The image: .Values.image.tag | default .Chart.AppVersion — default returns its argument if the piped value is empty; the tag is 2.7.2, so the line is image: "ghcr.io/myorg/web:2.7.2". (In production you would set a digest; k8s5.)
  7. {{- with .Values.resources }} sets the dot to the resources map and renders its body only if the map is non-empty. toYaml . serialises the map at column zero; nindent 10 places it under resources:.
  8. The checksum annotation renders the ConfigMap template itself to a string and takes its SHA-256. If config.LOG_LEVEL changes, the ConfigMap's rendered text changes, the hash changes, the pod template changes, and the Deployment rolls out new pods (k8s9). If nothing changes, the hash is identical and nothing rolls.

The rendered result (from helm template shop ./web -f values-prod.yaml --set image.tag=2.7.2):

apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: shop-web
  labels:
    app.kubernetes.io/name: web
    app.kubernetes.io/instance: shop
spec:
  replicas: 6
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app.kubernetes.io/name: web
      app.kubernetes.io/instance: shop
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app.kubernetes.io/name: web
        app.kubernetes.io/instance: shop
      annotations:
        checksum/config: 6f1c0b4e…   # sha256 of the rendered ConfigMap
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: web
        image: "ghcr.io/myorg/web:2.7.2"
        resources:
          limits:
            memory: 1Gi
          requests:
            cpu: "1"
            memory: 1Gi

Note toYaml sorted the keys alphabetically (limits before requests) and kept "1" quoted because it came from YAML as a string. Two classic template pitfalls come from types: --set converts true, numbers and null to typed values (use --set-string for literal strings), and large integers can be rendered in scientific notation if they pass through floating point. helm template plus a linter (helm lint, or validating the output with kubeconform) catches most of these before the cluster does.

4. Releases, upgrades and rollback

A release is one installation of a chart under a name in a namespace (shop in prod). Every install, upgrade or rollback creates a new revision, stored by default as a Secret in the release's namespace named sh.helm.release.v1.shop.v3, labelled owner=helm, containing the chart, the merged values and the rendered manifest (gzipped and base64-encoded). helm history shop lists the revisions with their status (deployed, superseded, failed, pending-upgrade); helm get values and helm get manifest read them back. Because the record is a Secret, it is subject to the 1 MiB object limit — very large charts can hit it.

On upgrade, Helm renders the new manifests and works out what to change. Helm 3 did this with a three-way merge: the old manifest from the last revision, the new manifest, and the live object, so that changes made in the cluster by others (an HPA's replica count, for example) are preserved unless the chart changes the same field. Helm 4, released in November 2025, switched new releases to Kubernetes server-side apply (k8s6): the API server merges the chart's fields and records Helm as their field manager, so a field owned by another manager produces an explicit conflict instead of a silent overwrite. Releases created by Helm 3 keep their original method when upgraded with Helm 4. Helm 3's final feature release is scheduled for September 2026, with security fixes through February 2027.

helm rollback shop 2 re-applies revision 2's manifests as a new revision (say, revision 5). It restores objects, not data. Two more gaps: Helm installs CRDs from a chart's crds/ directory on first install but never upgrades or deletes them, so CRD changes need their own process; and hooks — templates annotated helm.sh/hook: pre-upgrade and similar, typically Jobs for database migrations — run at defined points but are not themselves rolled back. A failed or interrupted upgrade can leave a release in pending-upgrade, blocking further operations with "another operation is in progress" until it is rolled back.

5. Kustomize: bases, overlays and generators

Kustomize takes the opposite approach: no templates. A kustomization.yaml lists resources and transformations, and kubectl kustomize (or kubectl apply -k) builds the result.

base/
  kustomization.yaml     # resources: [deployment.yaml, service.yaml, hpa.yaml]
  deployment.yaml        # a complete, valid Deployment (replicas omitted, image web:latest)
overlays/prod/
  kustomization.yaml
  resources-patch.yaml

# overlays/prod/kustomization.yaml
resources: [../../base]
namespace: prod
labels:
- pairs: { env: prod }
  includeSelectors: false
images:
- name: ghcr.io/myorg/web
  newTag: "2.7.2"
patches:
- path: resources-patch.yaml
configMapGenerator:
- name: web-config
  literals: [LOG_LEVEL=info]

# overlays/prod/resources-patch.yaml   (strategic merge patch)
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata: { name: web }
spec:
  template:
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: web                  # merged by container name
        resources:
          requests: { cpu: "1", memory: 1Gi }
          limits: { memory: 1Gi }

Building the prod overlay: Kustomize loads the base resources, sets metadata.namespace: prod on every object, adds the env: prod label, rewrites any image named ghcr.io/myorg/web to tag 2.7.2, and applies the patch with strategic merge semantics — Kubernetes-aware merging in which the containers list is merged by each container's name, so only web's resources change. (JSON 6902 patches with explicit op/path are available for precise edits.) The configMapGenerator creates a ConfigMap named web-config-<hash>, where the suffix is derived from a hash of its contents, and rewrites every reference to web-config in the Deployment to the hashed name. Change LOG_LEVEL and the name changes, so the pod template changes and pods roll — the same effect as Helm's checksum annotation, with old ConfigMaps left for rollbacks until pruned.

The appeal is that every file is ordinary YAML you can read, validate and diff; the limits are that anything not expressible as a patch or transformer — loops, conditionals, computed values — has no place, by design.
