Packaging and distributionVersioned charts, repos, OCI, dependenciesDirectories (remote bases by URL)
Release trackingRevisions, history, rollbackNone (left to Git / GitOps)
ReadabilityTemplates can be hard to readInputs are valid manifests
Typical useThird-party software; highly configurable appsYour own apps across environments

6. GitOps: the pull model

Helm and Kustomize decide what the manifests are. Something still has to apply them. Pushing from CI (helm upgrade in a pipeline) works but has two weaknesses: CI needs credentials that can change production, and nothing notices or corrects changes made outside the pipeline. GitOps, summarised by the OpenGitOps principles, fixes both: desired state is declarative, versioned and immutable (in Git), pulled automatically by agents, and continuously reconciled. It is the Kubernetes controller pattern (k8s6) applied one level up, with Git as the spec.

Argo CD has three main components. The repo-server clones repositories and renders manifests — plain YAML, Kustomize, Helm (via helm template) or plugins — caching results by commit. The application controller watches live objects in each destination cluster, compares them with the rendered desired state (normalising defaults so that fields the API server fills in do not count as drift), reports each Application as Synced or OutOfSync and Healthy, Progressing or Degraded, and performs syncs. The API server and UI serve users and CI. An Application declares it all:

apiVersion: argoproj.io/v1alpha1
kind: Application
metadata: { name: web-prod, namespace: argocd }
spec:
  project: shop
  source:
    repoURL: https://github.com/myorg/shop-config
    targetRevision: main
    path: web/overlays/prod
  destination: { server: https://kubernetes.default.svc, namespace: prod }
  syncPolicy:
    automated: { prune: true, selfHeal: true }
    syncOptions: [ServerSideApply=true]

With automated, a merge to main is noticed (by polling, every few minutes by default, or immediately via a webhook), rendered, diffed and applied. prune: true deletes live objects that disappeared from Git; selfHeal: true re-applies Git when someone changes the cluster by hand. Ordering within a sync uses sync waves (an annotation; lower waves are applied first and must become healthy before the next) and hooks (PreSync Jobs for migrations). AppProjects restrict which repositories, clusters and namespaces an Application may use — a security boundary that matters in the prod section. ApplicationSets generate Applications from patterns, such as one per directory or per cluster.

Flux takes the same approach with a toolkit of controllers: source-controller fetches GitRepository, OCIRepository and HelmRepository sources into artefacts; kustomize-controller applies Kustomization objects (Flux's resource, which builds a Kustomize directory and applies it with server-side apply, with pruning and health checks); helm-controller reconciles HelmRelease objects using the Helm libraries, so releases keep Helm's history; and image-automation controllers can commit new image tags back to Git. Argo CD is known for its UI and multi-cluster application view; Flux for composability and a Kubernetes-native, CLI-first design. Both are CNCF graduated projects.

7. Promotion, rollback and secrets in GitOps

A typical flow for one service:

  1. CI builds the image once, pushes it, signs it and records its digest (k8s5).
  2. CI opens a pull request (or commits directly, for dev) changing the image in overlays/dev to the new digest. Merge → Argo CD syncs dev.
  3. After dev checks pass, an automated pull request makes the same change in overlays/staging, then overlays/prod-eu, then overlays/prod-us, each gated on checks and, for production, approval. Only the version moves; environment differences stay in their overlays.
  4. Rollback is git revert of the promotion commit; the agent applies the previous digest. The Deployment performs an ordinary rolling update back (k8s7).

Secrets need care because Git must not hold plaintext. The common choices are SOPS (files encrypted with keys in a KMS, decrypted by the agent at render time — Flux supports it natively, Argo CD through plugins), Sealed Secrets (encrypted with a public key; only the controller in the cluster can decrypt into a Secret), or the External Secrets Operator, where Git holds an ExternalSecret that references a path in Vault or a cloud secret manager and the operator creates the Secret (k8s9). The last keeps secret material out of the GitOps pipeline entirely.

And one field needs special handling: replicas. If an HPA manages a Deployment, a replicas value in Git makes the agent reset it on every sync. Omit replicas from the manifest (the API server keeps the live value), or configure the tool to ignore it; with server-side apply, the HPA's controller owns the field and conflicts are visible.

8. A change, from commit to production, with times

Follow one change through a GitOps setup to see where time goes and where it can go wrong. At 10:00 a developer merges a fix to the application repository. CI builds, tests, scans and signs the image in about eight minutes, and at 10:08 opens a pull request in the configuration repository changing overlays/dev to the new digest; it is auto-merged because dev requires no review. Argo CD learns of the commit by webhook within seconds (without a webhook it polls, every three minutes by default), renders the overlay, sees the Deployment's pod template differ, and syncs at 10:09. The Deployment rolls out (k8s7) and is healthy by 10:11; Argo CD marks the Application Synced and Healthy. Automated checks run against dev, and at 10:20 a promotion pull request for staging opens; after the staging checks, a production pull request opens for one region, needs one approval, and is merged at 11:05. Production regions then follow one at a time.

Every step is visible and reversible: the commits say what changed and who approved it, the Application's history shows when each environment synced, and rollback at any stage is a revert. Two practical points come out of the timeline. Configure webhooks from the Git host to the GitOps agent, or "merged" and "deployed" can be minutes apart and confuse everyone. And keep promotion automated but gated: the value of GitOps is not speed alone but that the fast path and the safe path are the same path.

9. Laying out the configuration repository

Two layouts are common. A separate config repository holds the manifests or values for many services and environments; application repositories only build images, and CI opens pull requests against the config repository. This keeps deploy history in one place and lets platform teams review environment-wide changes. Keeping manifests next to the application code (a deploy/ directory) keeps a service self-contained, but then the deploy record is spread across repositories and an image build and its rollout are entangled in one commit. Whichever you choose, avoid one Git branch per environment: merging between long-lived environment branches drifts, conflicts and hides what is actually different; directories per environment (Kustomize overlays, values files) on one main branch make the differences explicit and diffable.
deep:
Templates versus overlays is a trade-off in where complexity lives

Templating puts complexity in the chart: every configurable field is a values key, and popular charts grow hundreds of keys, conditionals and helper functions until reading the template is harder than reading the output. Overlays put complexity in the variants: the base stays readable, but a large organisation can end up with deep chains of overlays whose combined effect is only visible after a build. Both converge on the same discipline: review the rendered output, not just the inputs. Tools that diff rendered manifests between the current and proposed commit in a pull request (Argo CD's diff, flux diff, helm diff) make the effect of a change visible where it is reviewed.

Server-side apply and field ownership

Server-side apply records, for every field of every object, which field manager last set it: Helm, Argo CD, the HPA controller, a human with kubectl. Applying a manifest that sets a field owned by another manager is a conflict; the applier must either drop the field or force ownership. This makes previously silent fights visible — GitOps versus HPA over replicas, a mutating webhook versus a chart over an injected sidecar — and makes "remove a field from Git" safe: with SSA, fields no longer in the applied configuration are removed if the manager owned them. The cost is learning to read managedFields and deciding deliberately which manager owns what.

Ordering, dependencies and CRDs

Kubernetes has no global transaction: a sync applies many objects, and some depend on others. A custom resource cannot be created before its CRD is established; a namespace must exist before objects in it; a migration Job should run before the new Deployment. Helm orders installs by kind with a built-in list and supports hooks and weights; Argo CD uses sync waves and phases; Flux uses dependsOn between Kustomizations and health checks. CRDs are the persistent pain point: they are cluster-scoped, shared by every release that uses them, and deleting one deletes every instance of it, so most platforms manage CRDs separately from the applications that use them, with conservative upgrade and no automatic pruning.

Multi-cluster and the app-of-apps pattern

With dozens of clusters, someone has to create the Argo CD Applications themselves. The app-of-apps pattern stores Application manifests in Git and has one root Application sync them; ApplicationSets generate Applications from generators (a list of clusters registered in Argo CD, directories in a repository, pull requests for preview environments). The same Git change can then fan out to every cluster in waves — one region first — which turns cluster-wide changes (a new admission policy, a CNI upgrade) into ordinary reviewed commits with a staged rollout, precisely the discipline whose absence caused the Reddit outage in sc15.

Charts are supply-chain inputs too

A third-party Helm chart is code that runs with your deployer's permissions: its templates decide which ClusterRoles, webhooks and privileged DaemonSets get created, and its hooks run Jobs at install time. Pulling latest of a popular chart from a public repository is the same risk as pulling an unpinned image (k8s5). Treat charts accordingly: pin chart versions (and, for OCI charts, digests), mirror them into an internal registry, verify provenance or signatures where publishers provide them, render and review the output of every upgrade — especially RBAC and admission-webhook changes — and scan rendered manifests with policy tools before they reach the cluster. The same applies to Kustomize remote bases referenced by URL.

Progressive delivery inside GitOps

GitOps decides what version should run; it does not, by itself, roll it out cautiously. Argo Rollouts and Flagger replace the Deployment's simple rolling update with canary or blue-green steps gated on metrics (swe9): a Rollout object in Git describes the steps (5% for five minutes, analysis, 25%…), and the controller shifts traffic through a service mesh or Gateway API weights (k8s8), aborting and scaling back the canary if the analysis fails. Git still holds the desired version; the rollout controller decides how fast reality catches up, and an aborted rollout leaves the cluster on the old version while Git says new — a deliberate, visible divergence for a human to resolve.

Rendering in CI versus rendering in the agent

Two schools exist for where manifests are rendered. In the first, the GitOps agent renders Helm charts and Kustomize overlays itself from source (Argo CD's repo-server, Flux's controllers). It keeps the repository small and declarative, but the exact manifests applied are only visible in the agent, and the renderer becomes a privileged component with access to many repositories — the risk the prod case illustrates. In the second, CI renders the final manifests and commits them (the "rendered manifests" pattern) to a branch or repository that the agent applies verbatim. Every change to what runs in the cluster is then a reviewable diff of plain YAML, and the agent no longer needs to execute templates or plugins, at the cost of more generated files in Git and a CI step that must stay in sync with tool versions. Teams with strict review requirements or many third-party charts increasingly prefer the second.
prod:
The case: Argo CD's Helm path traversal (CVE-2022-24348)

In February 2022 Argo CD published security advisory GHSA-63qx-x74g-jcr7, crediting Moshe Zioni of Apiiro with the discovery. Argo CD lets users create Applications whose source is a Helm chart, optionally with a list of values files. The repo-server renders such charts by running helm template with those values files on its own file system, where it keeps clones of every repository it serves. The advisory states that all versions were vulnerable to a path-traversal bug allowing arbitrary values files to be passed to Helm, and that while fixing it, the Argo CD team found that chart packages could also contain values files that were symbolic links pointing outside the repository root. A user allowed to create or update Applications, who knew or could guess the path of a YAML file on the repo-server, could therefore make a chart consume it as values and read data they had no right to — and because helm template's verbose error messages were returned to the user, they could enumerate files. The impact was especially critical where plugins such as git-crypt or SOPS decrypted secret value files to disk before rendering: other applications' secrets sat on the same disk. Fixed versions were 2.3.0, 2.2.4 and 2.1.9; there was no workaround.

The lesson connects to k8s9's subPath escape: a privileged component following paths and symlinks supplied by less-trusted users. For delivery systems specifically: the renderer runs other people's charts, plugins and Kustomize remote bases, so treat it as a sandbox boundary — restrict which repositories each team may use through AppProjects, avoid decrypting secrets to a shared file system (prefer External Secrets, where plaintext never passes through the GitOps pipeline), keep the agent patched, and limit what the agent's own credentials can do in each cluster.

Failure modes in production

  • "another operation (install/upgrade/rollback) is in progress": a Helm release stuck in pending-* after an interrupted upgrade. Roll back to the last deployed revision.
  • Immutable field changed: a chart change to a Deployment's selector or a StatefulSet's volumeClaimTemplates is rejected; requires delete-and-recreate or a new resource name.
  • Config changed, pods didn't: no checksum annotation or hashed ConfigMap name.
  • Sync loop / constant OutOfSync: fields defaulted or mutated by controllers and webhooks (replicas, injected sidecars, caBundles) not ignored or not owned via SSA.
  • Prune deletes too much: a refactor that moves resources between Applications deletes them in one and creates them in the other, briefly or with data loss for PVCs. Use prune-protection annotations on stateful resources.
  • Hotfix reverted: self-heal undoes an emergency kubectl change. Have a documented "pause sync" procedure and make the fix in Git.
  • CRD drift: chart upgrades that need newer CRDs fail because Helm does not upgrade them.

What to measure

Per Application: sync status, health, last sync time and duration, sync failures. For the pipeline: lead time from merge to synced in each environment, deployment frequency, change failure rate and time to restore (the DORA measures), drift events per week (a high number means people work around Git), and the age of the oldest unpromoted change between environments.

Ownership and access

Decide who may change what in the configuration repository with the same care as cluster RBAC, because in GitOps the repository is the access path to production. Code owners per directory, required reviews for production overlays, signed commits where your tooling supports them, and branch protection on the main branch translate organisational responsibility into enforceable rules, and the GitOps agent's AppProjects make sure a team's Applications can only deploy to that team's namespaces.
myths: Helm is a deployment tool that runs your application.

Helm renders templates into Kubernetes manifests and applies them, then records what it applied as a release. Everything after that — scheduling, rollouts, restarts — is done by Kubernetes controllers. helm upgrade returns when the API server has accepted the objects (or, with --wait, when they report ready), not when the application is healthy in any deeper sense.
helm rollback restores the previous state of the cluster.

It re-applies the manifests of an earlier release revision. Data changed by the newer version (database migrations, files on volumes), resources created outside the chart, and CRDs (which Helm does not upgrade or delete) are not rolled back. In GitOps setups, a Helm rollback also fights the Git source of truth unless Git is reverted too.
Kustomize is a template language.

Kustomize deliberately has no templating, variables or loops. It takes complete, valid YAML (a base) and applies declared transformations — patches, name prefixes, labels, image overrides, generated ConfigMaps — to produce variants. That makes every input a valid manifest you can read and diff, at the cost of less flexibility than templates.
GitOps means CI runs kubectl apply after merging.

In GitOps the cluster pulls: an agent running inside the cluster (Argo CD, Flux) continuously compares the cluster with Git and applies differences, and reverts changes made outside Git. CI pushing to the cluster lacks the continuous reconciliation and drift correction, and needs cluster credentials in the CI system.
Putting replicas in Git is always right for GitOps.

If an HPA manages a Deployment's replicas, a replicas value in Git makes the GitOps agent reset it on every sync, fighting the autoscaler. Leave replicas out of the manifest (the API server keeps the current value), or tell the tool to ignore that field.
Secrets can't be managed with GitOps.

Plain Secrets must not be committed, but encrypted forms can: SOPS-encrypted files decrypted by the agent, Sealed Secrets that only the cluster's controller can decrypt, or references to an external store resolved by the External Secrets Operator. Git then holds the declaration, not the plaintext.

recap: A Helm chart is a directory with Chart.yaml, default values.yaml and Go templates; helm renders templates with merged values (chart defaults, then -f files in order, then --set) and applies the result as a release.

Templates use the Go template language with Sprig functions; include, toYaml, nindent and whitespace trimming decide whether the output is valid YAML, and a checksum annotation of a ConfigMap makes pods roll when config changes.
Helm stores each release revision as a Secret (sh.helm.release.v1.<name>.v<N>) containing the chart, values and rendered manifest, which is what helm history and helm rollback use.

Helm 3 applied changes with a three-way merge; Helm 4 (November 2025) uses server-side apply for new releases, making ownership conflicts explicit; Helm 3's final feature release is September 2026 with security fixes into February 2027.
Kustomize builds variants from plain YAML: a base plus overlays that patch, rename, relabel and override images, and generators that add content-hash suffixes so config changes roll pods.
GitOps keeps desired state in Git and has an in-cluster agent pull, diff and apply it continuously, correcting drift; deploying is a merge and rolling back is a revert.

Argo CD's repo-server renders manifests (Helm, Kustomize, plain YAML), its application controller compares and syncs them, and Applications declare source, destination, sync policy, pruning and self-healing.
Flux does the same with separate controllers: source-controller fetches Git, OCI or Helm sources, kustomize-controller and helm-controller apply them.
Renderers and GitOps agents are privileged: CVE-2022-24348 let a crafted Helm chart make Argo CD's repo-server read values files outside the repository, exposing other applications' secrets.
glossary: Application (Argo CD)
A custom resource naming a source (repository, path, revision, Helm or Kustomize settings), a destination cluster and namespace, and a sync policy.
base / overlay
In Kustomize, a base is a set of resources; an overlay references a base and applies environment-specific changes to it.
chart
A Helm package: templates, default values and metadata, distributed as a directory, a .tgz archive or an OCI artefact.
drift
A difference between the desired state in Git and the live state in the cluster, usually from manual changes.
Flux
A CNCF GitOps toolkit of controllers (source, kustomize, helm, notification, image automation) that reconcile clusters from Git or OCI sources.
generator (Kustomize)
A Kustomize feature that creates ConfigMaps or Secrets from files or literals, adding a hash of the content to the name.
GitOps
Operating a system by declaring its desired state in Git and letting automated agents pull and continuously reconcile it.
Helm hook
A template annotated to run at a point in a release's life (pre-install, post-upgrade…), often a Job such as a migration.
helper (named template)
A reusable template defined with define in _helpers.tpl and inserted with include, such as the chart's full name or common labels.
OpenGitOps principles
Declarative, versioned and immutable, pulled automatically, continuously reconciled.
prune
Deleting live resources that are no longer present in the desired state.
release (Helm)
An installed instance of a chart with a name and a revision history, stored in the cluster.
repo-server
The Argo CD component that clones repositories and renders manifests with Helm, Kustomize or plugins.
self-heal
A GitOps agent re-applying the desired state when someone changes the live cluster by hand.
sync
Applying the rendered desired state to the cluster so live matches Git.
sync wave
An Argo CD annotation that orders resources during a sync, applying lower waves first and waiting for them to be healthy.
values
The configuration inputs of a Helm chart, merged from defaults, files and command-line overrides.
drill:
Diagnose: the deployment that keeps undoing itself

A team moved a service to Argo CD with automated sync, prune and self-heal. Since then: (1) every few minutes the Deployment's replicas drop from around 12 to 3 and climb back, and users see brief latency spikes; (2) a ConfigMap change merged an hour ago is visible in the cluster, but the pods still log with the old level; (3) during last night's incident an engineer raised a memory limit with kubectl edit, and it reverted within three minutes, causing OOM kills to resume. The manifests are plain YAML in a Kustomize overlay with replicas: 3, a ConfigMap web-config referenced by envFrom, and an HPA. Explain each symptom and fix them.

Answer

(1) The HPA scales to ~12, Argo CD sees replicas: 3 in Git, reports OutOfSync and self-heal applies 3; the HPA scales up again. Fix: remove replicas from the overlay (or add ignoreDifferences for /spec/replicas), and use server-side apply so the HPA owns the field. (2) The ConfigMap object changed, but the pods read it through envFrom, which is evaluated only at container start, and the pod template did not change, so no rollout happened. Fix: replace the plain ConfigMap with a configMapGenerator so its name carries a content hash and references update, causing a rollout on every config change (or add a checksum annotation if using Helm). (3) Self-heal did exactly its job: the live object differed from Git. Fix the process, not the tool: the emergency change should be a commit (fast-tracked review), or the runbook should include pausing automated sync for that Application (disable self-heal or the automated policy temporarily) and re-enabling it after the fix lands in Git. Raise the memory limit in the overlay now, so the incident fix is permanent. Add alerts on repeated self-heal events, which reveal both automation fights and people working around Git.
qa: E
What problem do Helm and Kustomize solve?

Real applications need many manifests, and the same application runs in several environments with small differences: replicas, image tags, resources, hostnames. Copying YAML per environment drifts and is error-prone. Helm templates the manifests and fills them from values per environment; Kustomize keeps one plain base and applies declared patches per environment. Both produce ordinary Kubernetes objects.
E
What is in a Helm chart?

Chart.yaml (name, version, appVersion, dependencies), values.yaml (default configuration), templates/ (Go templates that render manifests, plus _helpers.tpl for named templates and NOTES.txt), and optionally charts/ for subchart dependencies, a values schema and CRDs in crds/. helm template renders it locally; helm install or upgrade renders and applies it as a release.
E
What is GitOps?

A way of operating where the desired state of the system lives in Git, and an agent running in the cluster pulls it, compares it with the live state and applies differences continuously, also reverting manual changes. Deploying means merging a change, rolling back means reverting a commit, and Git history is the audit log.
M
Walk through how Helm renders a value into a Deployment.

Helm merges values: the chart's values.yaml, then each -f file in order, then --set flags, later overriding earlier. It then executes each template with a context containing .Values, .Release, .Chart and .Capabilities. {{ .Values.replicaCount }} becomes 3; include of a named helper produces the full name; toYaml of the resources map, piped to nindent 12, emits correctly indented YAML; {{- trims whitespace. The rendered documents are parsed as YAML and sent to the API server, and the release record stores them.
Follow-up: Why does a missing nindent cause errors? — toYaml output starts at column zero, so without re-indenting the lines land outside their parent key and the YAML is invalid or silently wrong.
M
How does helm rollback work, and what does it not undo?

Each upgrade creates a new revision, stored as a Secret holding the chart, values and rendered manifests. helm rollback web 2 re-applies revision 2's manifests as a new revision. It does not undo data changes made by the newer version, resources created outside the chart, or CRD changes, which Helm does not manage on upgrade. In GitOps setups you revert Git instead, or the agent will re-apply the newer version.
M
How do you make pods restart when a ConfigMap changes?

Pods that read configuration as environment variables never see changes, and file-mounted values change only eventually and need reloading. Helm charts commonly put an annotation on the pod template containing the sha256 of the rendered ConfigMap; Kustomize's configMapGenerator puts a content hash in the ConfigMap's name and updates references. Either way, a config change changes the pod template, so the Deployment rolls out new pods.
M
Compare Helm and Kustomize.

Helm templates manifests with a full template language, packages them as versioned charts with dependencies, and tracks releases with history and rollback; it is the standard way to distribute software to others. Kustomize patches plain YAML without templates, is built into kubectl, and is good for your own applications' environment variants. Many teams use both: third-party software via Helm charts, their own apps via Kustomize, sometimes Kustomize patching Helm output.
M
How do you promote a release through environments with GitOps?

CI builds and pushes an image by digest, then updates the desired version for the first environment in the config repository, by commit or pull request. The GitOps agent syncs it. After checks pass, a promotion is another commit changing the next environment's version — often an automated pull request. Rollback is reverting the commit. Environment differences live in overlays or values files, so promotion changes only the version.
M
What do Argo CD's prune and self-heal do, and what are the risks?

Prune deletes live resources that were removed from Git; self-heal re-applies Git when someone changes the live cluster. Together they make Git authoritative. Risks: a bad commit that removes a directory can delete production resources, so use prune with care, deletion protection annotations and review; and self-heal reverts emergency hotfixes made with kubectl, so hotfixes must go through Git, with a documented way to pause sync during incidents.
H
Explain CVE-2022-24348 and what it teaches about GitOps tooling.

Argo CD's repo-server renders Helm charts for any Application a user may create or update. It accepted values-file paths that traversed outside the repository and, as the team found while fixing it, value files that were symlinks inside a chart package. A user with permission to create Applications could point a chart at any YAML file on the repo-server, including decrypted secrets of other applications when SOPS or git-crypt plugins decrypt to disk, and use verbose helm template errors to enumerate files. Fixed in 2.1.9, 2.2.4 and 2.3.0. Lesson: rendering untrusted inputs is code execution-adjacent; isolate renderers, restrict who can create Applications and from which repositories (AppProjects), and avoid decrypting secrets to shared disk.
H
An HPA and Argo CD fight over a Deployment's replicas. Why, and how do you fix it?

The manifest in Git sets replicas: 3. The HPA scales to 10; Argo CD sees drift from Git and, with self-heal, resets it to 3; the HPA scales back up, and so on, causing pod churn. Fix by removing replicas from the manifest so the API server keeps the current value on apply, or configuring ignoreDifferences for /spec/replicas, and with server-side apply, letting the HPA own that field.
H
Design the delivery system for 40 microservices across dev, staging and three production regions.

One config repository (or one per team) with a Kustomize base or Helm values per service and overlays per environment and region; CI builds images, signs them and opens pull requests updating digests for dev; promotion to staging and then each production region is an automated pull request gated on checks and, for production, approval. Argo CD with ApplicationSets generates one Application per service per cluster from the directory structure; AppProjects restrict which repositories and namespaces each team can deploy; sync waves order CRDs and migrations; progressive delivery with Argo Rollouts for the riskiest services; secrets via External Secrets. Production regions are promoted one at a time.
Follow-up: What would you monitor? — Sync status and health per Application, time from merge to synced, drift events, and failed syncs, plus deployment frequency and change failure rate.
refs: Path traversal and symlinked values files in Helm charts rendered by the repo-server; fixed in 2.1.9, 2.2.4 and 2.3.0.
Built-in objects, values, functions and pipelines, named templates, whitespace control.
Helm 4.0 (November 2025): server-side apply for new releases and other changes from Helm 3.
Bases, overlays, patches, generators and kubectl apply -k.
Architecture, Applications, sync options, sync waves, ApplicationSets and projects.
Source, kustomize and helm controllers, and image automation.
The four principles: declarative, versioned and immutable, pulled automatically, continuously reconciled.

t: Debugging Kubernetes: CrashLoopBackOff, OOMKilled, ImagePullBackOff, probes and kubectl techniques
sum: A systematic way to debug workloads: read status, events and last state; decode exit codes; work through Pending, ContainerCreating, ImagePullBackOff, CrashLoopBackOff, OOMKilled, probe failures, Running-but-not-Ready and stuck Terminating, each traced from real kubectl describe output; and the tools — logs --previous, events, ephemeral debug containers, node debugging — with Zalando's liveness-probe lessons and the Kubernetes Failure Stories as the case.
prereq: k8s6
The scheduler binds pods; the kubelet runs them through the CRI and reports status; components record events; the API server is the single source of truth.
k8s7
Pods have phases, conditions and per-container states; restart policies restart exited containers; Deployments roll out ReplicaSets.
k8s10
Exceeding a memory limit gets a container OOM-killed with exit code 137; node pressure triggers eviction; requests decide scheduling.
k8s8
Services route to ready pods through EndpointSlices; DNS resolves Service names; NetworkPolicy can block traffic.
why:
It is 2 a.m. and the pager says checkout is failing. kubectl get pods shows a column of words — CrashLoopBackOff, 0/1 Running, ImagePullBackOff, Pending, Terminating — and a restart count of 47. The engineer on call tries kubectl logs and gets two lines of start-up banner. They try kubectl exec … bash and get "executable file not found", because the image is distroless. They restart the Deployment, which makes everything worse for ten minutes. The cause, when they find it an hour later, was printed in plain text all along — in the previous container's logs, in the Last State section of kubectl describe, in an event that said exactly which Secret key was missing.

Debugging Kubernetes is less about clever tricks than about knowing where each kind of failure leaves its evidence. Every component in k8s6 writes something down: the scheduler records why a pod could not be placed; the kubelet records image pulls, probe failures, kills and back-offs as events and as the container's last state; the kernel's OOM killer leaves a reason and an exit code; controllers record what they created and why they stalled. A small number of commands reads all of it, and a small number of patterns covers most incidents.

Some failures are made worse by Kubernetes' own machinery when it is configured carelessly. The best-known example is the liveness probe that checks a database: one slow query, and the kubelet restarts every replica of every service at once. Zalando's engineers, who run hundreds of clusters, wrote this up in 2019 under the title "Liveness Probes are Dangerous" and started a public collection of Kubernetes failure stories so that others could learn from such incidents without repeating them.

This lesson gives a systematic method — follow the pod's life from scheduling to serving and ask, at each stage, "did this step happen, and if not, what does the evidence say?" — and then works through each common state with real kubectl describe output: Pending, ContainerCreating, ImagePullBackOff, CreateContainerConfigError, CrashLoopBackOff (with exit codes decoded), OOMKilled, probe failures, Running but not Ready, Ready but failing, and stuck Terminating. It ends with the toolkit for images without shells and for node-level problems, and with what to put in place so the next 2 a.m. is shorter.
primer:
A parcel's tracking page

When a parcel goes missing you do not search every warehouse. You open the tracking page and find the last scan: "accepted", "sorted", "out for delivery", "delivery attempted — no access". The last successful step tells you where to look, and the failed step usually comes with a reason.

A pod has the same kind of tracking history, and the stages always happen in the same order:

The tracking page itself is three commands. kubectl get pods gives the one-word summary per pod: STATUS, READY, RESTARTS. kubectl describe pod gives the full record: each container's current state and Last State (the previous run's exit code and reason), the pod's conditions, and the most recent events for that pod. kubectl logs --previous gives what the crashed instance printed before it died. Most incidents are solved by reading these three in order, before touching anything.

Who wrote each clue

Every line of evidence was written by one component, and knowing which tells you how far the pod got. A FailedScheduling event comes from the scheduler: the pod never reached a node. FailedMount, Pulling, BackOff, Unhealthy and Killing come from the kubelet on the pod's node: the pod is bound and the node is trying. OOMKilled in Last State was recorded by the runtime after the kernel killed the process. SuccessfulCreate or FailedCreate on a ReplicaSet comes from its controller: if pods do not even exist, look there, because an admission webhook or a quota may have refused them. The From column in the events table is therefore as informative as the message, and a missing kind of event — no scheduler event at all, no kubelet events — points straight at the component that is not doing its job.

The second habit is to stop before "fixing". Restarting pods, deleting them or scaling up destroys evidence — the previous container's logs, the last state, the pod that showed the problem — and in some failure modes (liveness cascades, overloaded dependencies) makes the outage worse. Read first, then act; if users are hurting, roll back the last change (k8s7), which is usually safer than any improvised fix.

Where the analogy breaks: a tracking page keeps its history forever, but Kubernetes events are kept for only about an hour by default, logs of a container are only kept for the current and previous instance, and a deleted pod takes its status with it. Evidence evaporates, so capture it early — and ship events and logs somewhere durable before you need them.
body:
1. The core commands and what each one shows

CommandShowsUse it for
kubectl get pods -o wideStatus, ready count, restarts, node, IPWhich pods, where, how bad
kubectl describe pod PContainer states and Last State, conditions, eventsThe "why" for almost every state
kubectl logs P [-c C] --previousOutput of the crashed instanceCrash causes the app printed
kubectl get events -n NS --sort-by=.lastTimestampEverything recorded in the namespaceScheduling, pulls, kills, controller actions
kubectl describe deploy/rs/stsController conditions and eventsRollouts that stall, pods never created
kubectl get pod P -o yamlFull spec and statusExact fields: probes, env, resources
kubectl debug …Shell with tools next to the app or on the nodeImages without shells, network and node checks
kubectl top pod/nodeCurrent CPU and memory (metrics-server)Resource pressure at a glance

One thing to know about kubectl get pods: the STATUS column is a convenience computed by kubectl from the pod's phase and container states, not a field in the API. "CrashLoopBackOff", "ImagePullBackOff", "Init:0/2" and "Terminating" are not phases; the phase is still Pending or Running. Read the container states in describe for the real picture.

2. Exit codes: decode before you read logs

When a container stops, its process's exit status is recorded. Shells and runtimes use the convention that a process killed by signal N reports 128 + N. That makes the last state's exit code the fastest clue:

Exit codeMeaningTypical cause in Kubernetes
0SuccessA process that should keep running exited (wrong command, daemon that forks to background)
1, 2 …The application's own errorConfiguration missing, dependency unreachable at start, unhandled exception
126Command cannot be executedNot executable, wrong permissions
127Command not foundTypo in command, binary missing in image, shell-form command in a shell-less image
128 + 9 = 137SIGKILLOOM kill (reason OOMKilled), or killed after grace period (liveness failure, deletion, eviction)
128 + 11 = 139SIGSEGVNative crash: segfault in a C extension, incompatible library or architecture
128 + 15 = 143SIGTERMStopped gracefully on request (deletion, liveness restart with a handler)

The reason next to the exit code narrows it further: OOMKilled (the kernel, k8s10), Error (non-zero exit), Completed (exit 0), ContainerCannotRun or StartError (the runtime could not start the process at all — exec format errors from wrong-architecture images, k8s1, land here). Applications can also write a short explanation to /dev/termination-log, which appears as the termination message.

3. CrashLoopBackOff, worked

When a container exits and the pod's restart policy says to restart it, the kubelet does — after a delay that starts at 10 seconds and doubles each time (20, 40, 80, 160 s) up to a cap of 5 minutes, and resets once the container has run successfully for 10 minutes. While waiting, the container's state is Waiting with reason CrashLoopBackOff. (Kubernetes 1.33 added alpha options to shorten this — a 1-second initial delay and 60-second cap, or a per-node maximum — but the defaults above apply unless your cluster enables them.)

Here is a real-shaped kubectl describe pod for a crash-looping API (trimmed):

Name:         api-6b7d9c5f4-q8xkz
Namespace:    shop
Status:       Running
Containers:
  api:
    Image:          ghcr.io/myorg/api@sha256:3f9c…
    State:          Waiting
      Reason:       CrashLoopBackOff
    Last State:     Terminated
      Reason:       Error
      Exit Code:    1
      Started:      Sat, 04 Oct 2026 02:11:40 +0000
      Finished:     Sat, 04 Oct 2026 02:11:42 +0000
    Ready:          False
    Restart Count:  6
    Environment Variables from:
      api-config    ConfigMap  Optional: false
Conditions:
  Ready             False
Events:
  Type     Reason     Age                  From     Message
  ----     ------     ----                 ----     -------
  Normal   Pulled     7m (x7 over 13m)     kubelet  Container image "ghcr.io/myorg/api@sha256:3f9c…" already present on machine
  Normal   Created    7m (x7 over 13m)     kubelet  Created container: api
  Normal   Started    7m (x7 over 13m)     kubelet  Started container api
  Warning  BackOff    2m (x26 over 12m)    kubelet  Back-off restarting failed container api in pod api-6b7d9c5f4-q8xkz

Read it top to bottom. The image is present and the container is created and started each time, so stages 1-3 are fine. Last State says the previous run lasted two seconds and exited with code 1 and reason Error: the application itself gave up, not the kernel or the kubelet. Restart count 6 over 13 minutes matches the back-off schedule. Nothing about probes. So the answer is in the application's output:

$ kubectl logs api-6b7d9c5f4-q8xkz --previous
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "/app/api/settings.py", line 14, in <module>
    DATABASE_URL = os.environ["DATABASE_URL"]
KeyError: 'DATABASE_URL'

The new release renamed the variable in the ConfigMap to DB_URL. Fix the ConfigMap or the code and roll forward, or kubectl rollout undo while you do. Without --previous, kubectl logs would have shown the current instance, which in the waiting state has no output at all.

Three other common shapes of the same state:

  • Exit code 0, reason Completed, still CrashLoopBackOff: the process finished successfully but the restart policy is Always. The command runs a one-shot script, or a daemon forks to the background and the foreground process exits. Make the main process stay in the foreground, or use a Job (k8s7).
  • Exit code 127 or 126: the command does not exist or cannot run in this image — a typo in command, a shell-form command in a distroless image (k8s3), a script without execute permission.
  • Exit code 139: a native crash. Common after a base-image change that brought an incompatible library, or an image built for another architecture under emulation.

4. OOMKilled

    Last State:     Terminated
      Reason:       OOMKilled
      Exit Code:    137
      Started:      Sat, 04 Oct 2026 01:52:03 +0000
      Finished:     Sat, 04 Oct 2026 02:06:47 +0000
    Restart Count:  3
    Limits:
      memory:  2Gi
    Requests:
      cpu:     500m
      memory:  2Gi

The container ran for about fifteen minutes and was killed by the kernel for exceeding its 2 GiB limit (k8s10). The application logs usually end mid-sentence: there was no chance to log anything. Questions to answer:

  1. Growth or spike? Graph container_memory_working_set_bytes for the pod: a steady climb over the fifteen minutes is a leak or an unbounded cache; a sudden jump is one large request, a batch job or a data load.
  2. What kind of memory? From a debug container or the node, read the cgroup's memory.stat: large anon is heap; large shmem is /dev/shm or memory-backed emptyDirs (data-loader workers); large file is page cache that could not be reclaimed fast enough.
  3. Does the runtime know its limit? A JVM, Node.js or a worker pool sized from the node's memory rather than the container's will overshoot (k8s3).
  4. Is the limit simply too low for the real workload? If usage is legitimate, raise the limit — and the request with it.

Distinguish this from eviction, where the pod (not just the container) is terminated by the kubelet under node pressure: the pod's status shows reason: Evicted and a message such as "The node was low on resource: memory", and its controller creates a replacement elsewhere.

5. Image pull failures

Events:
  Warning  Failed     12s (x3 over 52s)  kubelet  Failed to pull image "ghcr.io/myorg/api:2.7.3": failed to resolve reference "ghcr.io/myorg/api:2.7.3": ghcr.io/myorg/api:2.7.3: not found
  Warning  Failed     12s (x3 over 52s)  kubelet  Error: ErrImagePull
  Normal   BackOff    1s (x4 over 51s)   kubelet  Back-off pulling image "ghcr.io/myorg/api:2.7.3"
  Warning  Failed     1s (x4 over 51s)   kubelet  Error: ImagePullBackOff

ErrImagePull is a failed attempt; ImagePullBackOff is the wait before the next one (with the same doubling back-off). The registry's message decides the fix:

  • not found / manifest unknown: wrong repository or tag, or CI never pushed it. Check with docker buildx imagetools inspect or crane manifest from outside the cluster.
  • unauthorized / 403 / pull access denied: private registry without credentials. Add imagePullSecrets (a kubernetes.io/dockerconfigjson Secret) to the pod or its service account, or configure node-level credentials.
  • toomanyrequests: registry rate limit (Docker Hub, k8s5). Authenticate or use a mirror.
  • i/o timeout, no such host: the node cannot reach the registry: DNS, egress firewall, proxy, private endpoint.
  • no matching manifest for linux/arm64: the image has no variant for the node's architecture (k8s1).

6. Pending, ContainerCreating and configuration errors

Pending with FailedScheduling. The scheduler explains itself:

  Warning  FailedScheduling  30s  default-scheduler  0/6 nodes are available: 2 node(s) had untolerated taint {nvidia.com/gpu: present}, 4 Insufficient memory. preemption: 0/6 nodes are available: 6 No preemption victims found for incoming pod.

Six nodes: two are GPU nodes the pod does not tolerate, four lack enough unrequested memory for its request, and nothing lower-priority could be preempted. Options: reduce the request if it is inflated, add capacity (or check why the autoscaler did not, k8s11), or add a toleration if the pod belongs on GPU nodes. Other common reasons in the same message: didn't match Pod's node affinity/selector, didn't match pod topology spread constraints, had volume node affinity conflict, pod has unbound immediate PersistentVolumeClaims (k8s9). No event at all means no scheduler has looked at it (k8s6's drill).

ContainerCreating for minutes. The pod is bound but the kubelet cannot finish preparing it. Events name the step: FailedMount or FailedAttachVolume (a volume, often a Multi-Attach error or a missing Secret volume, k8s9), FailedCreatePodSandBox with a CNI error (no IPs left, the CNI DaemonSet not running on that node, k8s8).

CreateContainerConfigError. The kubelet could not assemble the container's configuration, so it never started it:

  Warning  Failed  5s (x4 over 40s)  kubelet  Error: couldn't find key DATABASE_URL in Secret shop/db

or container has runAsNonRoot and image has non-numeric user (app), cannot verify user is non-root (k8s3). The message is exact; fix the reference.

7. Probes: when health checks cause the failure

Probes (sc15, k8s7) are run by the kubelet with defaults of periodSeconds: 10, timeoutSeconds: 1, successThreshold: 1, failureThreshold: 3. A liveness failure looks like this:

  Warning  Unhealthy  40s (x3 over 60s)  kubelet  Liveness probe failed: Get "http://10.244.1.17:8080/healthz": context deadline exceeded (Client.Timeout exceeded while awaiting headers)
  Normal   Killing    40s                kubelet  Container api failed liveness probe, will be restarted

The probe timed out three times in a row (one second each), so the kubelet killed the container: SIGTERM, then SIGKILL after the grace period, giving exit code 143 or 137 with reason Error — easily mistaken for an OOM. Ask why /healthz took more than a second. If the app was busy (CPU saturated, throttled by a CPU limit, k8s10, or in a long garbage-collection pause), the liveness probe has just restarted a slow but working container, losing its in-flight requests and its warm cache, and the remaining pods now carry more load and may fail their probes too. If /healthz checks the database, a database slowdown fails every pod's liveness at once.

The rules that prevent this: liveness checks only that the process can make progress (a trivial local endpoint, no dependencies); thresholds and timeouts generous enough to survive GC pauses and load spikes (for example timeoutSeconds: 5, failureThreshold: 6); readiness — which removes the pod from traffic instead of killing it — is where dependency and overload checks belong; a startupProbe protects slow starters, so the liveness probe does not kill a JVM that needs 60 seconds to warm up; and many services are better off with no liveness probe at all.

Running but not Ready is the readiness probe failing:

  Warning  Unhealthy  3s (x40 over 6m)  kubelet  Readiness probe failed: HTTP probe failed with statuscode: 503

The pod is out of the Service's endpoints and receives no traffic. Check the probe's port and path against what the app really serves (a port renamed in the new release, a health path that moved), whether the app is still warming up, and whether readiness depends on a failing downstream — in which case every pod is unready and the Service has no endpoints at all.

8. Ready, but the service still fails

If pods are Running, Ready and not restarting, but clients see errors, move down the path traffic takes (k8s8):

  1. Endpoints. kubectl get endpointslices -l kubernetes.io/service-name=api. Empty, or missing the new pods, means the Service's selector does not match the pods' labels, or targetPort names a port the pods do not have.
  2. From inside. Start a debug pod (kubectl run -it --rm dbg --image=nicolaka/netshoot -- bash) and test in layers: curl <pod-ip>:8080 (the app), curl api.shop:80 (Service and DNS), nslookup api.shop (DNS alone). The first layer that fails is the culprit.
  3. Policy. If direct pod access fails only from some namespaces, a NetworkPolicy is likely; check policies selecting the pods and the caller's egress.
  4. Entry point. For external traffic, the Gateway's and HTTPRoute's status conditions say whether the route is accepted and its backends resolved; the load balancer's health checks say whether nodes or pods are considered healthy.
  5. The application. Logs, metrics and traces — the cluster may be fine and the bug in the code; kubectl port-forward pod/api-… 8080 lets you hit one pod directly from your laptop.

9. Debugging without a shell: kubectl debug

Distroless and minimal images (k8s3) have no shell or tools. Ephemeral containers solve this by adding a temporary container to a running pod:

kubectl debug -it pod/api-6b7d9c5f4-q8xkz --image=busybox:1.37 --target=api -- sh
/ # ps aux                       # sees the api process (shared process namespace via --target)
/ # ls /proc/1/root/app          # the api container's file system
/ # wget -qO- localhost:8080/healthz   # same network namespace as the pod

The ephemeral container shares the pod's network namespace, so localhost is the app; with --target it also joins the target container's process namespace, so it can see the app's processes and, through /proc/<pid>/root, its files and mounted Secrets (which is why creating ephemeral containers requires its own RBAC permission). Ephemeral containers cannot be removed and have no resource limits or probes; they disappear with the pod. Two variants: kubectl debug pod/X --copy-to=X-debug --set-image=api=busybox:1.37 or --share-processes creates a modified copy of the pod (useful when the original crashes too fast to attach to, since you can change its command to sleep); and kubectl debug node/worker-3 -it --image=ubuntu runs a privileged-enough pod in the node's host namespaces with the node's root file system mounted at /host, from which chroot /host, crictl ps, journalctl -u kubelet and the cgroup files are reachable. --profile (general, baseline, restricted, netadmin, sysadmin) chooses the security settings of the debug container.

10. Stuck Terminating

A pod that stays Terminating long after its grace period usually has one of two causes. Its node is gone or unreachable, so no kubelet will ever confirm the containers stopped (k8s6); the pod object waits, which for StatefulSets is a deliberate safety guarantee (k8s7). Or it has finalizers — keys in metadata.finalizers that block deletion until a controller removes them after cleanup — and the controller responsible is not running. The same applies to namespaces stuck terminating, usually because of custom resources whose operator was deleted first. kubectl delete --force --grace-period=0 removes the pod object without waiting for confirmation; if the node is actually alive, the containers may keep running while a replacement starts, which for anything with a volume or a unique identity is how split-brain happens. Find the cause first; force deletion is the last step.

11. kubectl techniques that save time

A few commands turn the method into seconds rather than minutes. kubectl get pods -A --field-selector=status.phase=Pending lists every pending pod in the cluster; kubectl get pods -o wide --sort-by=.status.containerStatuses[0].restartCount puts the restart-heavy ones last. kubectl events --for pod/api-6b7d9c5f4-q8xkz --types=Warning shows only that pod's warnings, and kubectl get events -A --field-selector type=Warning --sort-by=.lastTimestamp gives a cluster-wide incident view. JSONPath extracts exactly the field you need, for example kubectl get pod P -o jsonpath='{range .status.containerStatuses[*]}{.name}{" "}{.lastState.terminated.reason}{" "}{.lastState.terminated.exitCode}{"\n"}{end}' to list each container's last termination reason and code. kubectl logs -l app=api --prefix --since=10m reads recent logs from every pod of a service at once. kubectl rollout history and kubectl rollout status --timeout=120s tie symptoms to the release that caused them. kubectl wait --for=condition=Ready pod -l app=api --timeout=60s makes scripts and runbooks wait correctly instead of sleeping. kubectl auth can-i create pods/ephemeralcontainers -n shop tells you whether you are allowed to debug before you try. And adding -v=6 (or -v=8 for bodies) to any command shows the API calls it makes, which settles "is it kubectl, RBAC or the API server?" in one line.

These are worth putting into a team runbook with the outputs annotated, because at 2 a.m. nobody remembers JSONPath syntax, and a runbook that turns "read Last State for every container" into one pasted command is the difference between a ten-minute and an hour-long diagnosis.
deep:
Events are lossy; plan for it

Events are ordinary API objects with a time-to-live (one hour by default, set on the API server), and repeated events are aggregated into counts ("x26 over 12m"). Under load, components rate-limit event creation, and big clusters often store events in a separate etcd to protect the main one. The consequences: events for an incident that happened overnight are gone by morning, and events for a burst may be incomplete. Production platforms export events to their logging system with an event exporter, so incident timelines can be reconstructed, and alert on warning events by reason (BackOff, FailedScheduling, FailedMount, Unhealthy) rather than waiting for someone to run describe.

Logs live on the node

Container output goes to files on the node, managed by the kubelet and runtime (under /var/log/pods/), rotated at a size limit (10 MiB per file by default) and keeping a few files. kubectl logs streams them through the API server and kubelet. Only the current and previous container instances are reachable; earlier crashes, deleted pods and pods on dead nodes take their logs with them. That is why cluster-level log collection (a DaemonSet shipping files to a central store) is part of any real platform, and why applications should log to stdout and stderr rather than to files inside the container, which no one collects and which fill the writable layer (k8s2).

Signals, grace periods and what the app sees

Every way a container is stopped by Kubernetes — deletion, rollout, scale-down, eviction, preemption, liveness failure, node drain — goes through the same sequence: preStop hook, then SIGTERM to PID 1, then SIGKILL after terminationGracePeriodSeconds (k8s1, k8s7). The exit code tells you whether the app exited on SIGTERM (143) or had to be killed (137). Seeing 137 with reason Error on every rollout means the app ignores SIGTERM, which also means in-flight requests are cut off on every deploy; fix PID 1 before chasing anything else. The termination reason, events from the component that initiated the stop (kubelet, scheduler for preemption, eviction API, Karpenter or the cluster autoscaler) and the timing pattern together identify who pulled the trigger.

Debugging the node and the runtime

Some failures are below the pod: a kubelet that cannot talk to the API server (expired certificates), a container runtime that hangs, a full disk, exhausted PIDs or inodes, a kernel bug. Node conditions (MemoryPressure, DiskPressure, PIDPressure, Ready) summarise the kubelet's view; the Node Problem Detector adds conditions and events for kernel deadlocks, file-system corruption and runtime problems. From a node debug pod: journalctl -u kubelet -u containerd, crictl ps -a and crictl logs for containers the API no longer shows, df -h and df -i, and dmesg for OOM-killer reports and hardware errors. When a node is sick in ways that are hard to fix, cordon, drain and replace it; nodes are cattle.

Admission and quota: failures before a pod exists

Sometimes there is no failing pod to describe, because the pod was never created. A Deployment shows fewer ready replicas than desired, and kubectl get pods shows nothing new. The ReplicaSet's events explain it: FailedCreate … exceeded quota (a ResourceQuota on the namespace), violates PodSecurity "restricted" (Pod Security Admission rejected the template), or admission webhook … denied the request (a policy engine such as Kyverno). Because these rejections happen in the API server's write path (k8s6), they appear on the controller that tried to create the pod, not on any pod — a common blind spot when people only ever describe pods.

Making the next incident shorter

The most effective debugging work happens before the incident. Structured logs with request IDs; metrics for every service's request rate, errors and latency; traces across services; events and logs exported off-cluster; dashboards for restarts, OOM kills, throttling and pending pods; alerts on symptoms users feel rather than on every warning event; runbooks for the states in this lesson; and a habit of rolling back first and debugging second when users are affected. And the design rules that prevent whole classes of incident: safe probes, PID 1 that handles SIGTERM, accurate requests, memory limits equal to requests, and images that identify their source.

Reproducing a failure safely

When a failure cannot be understood from the evidence, reproduce it outside production rather than experimenting on the live service. kubectl get pod P -o yaml gives the exact spec; strip the status and node-specific fields and apply it in a staging namespace with the same image digest, ConfigMaps and Secrets (or safe copies), and the same resource limits. A crash that reproduces there can be investigated freely: change the command to sleep and step through start-up with a debug container, lower the memory limit to trigger the OOM on purpose, or point the readiness probe at the endpoint you suspect. A crash that does not reproduce narrows the cause to something about the production environment — data, traffic, a dependency, the node — which is itself a strong clue.
prod:
The case: "Liveness Probes are Dangerous" and the Kubernetes Failure Stories

Henning Jacobs, then at Zalando, which operated a large fleet of Kubernetes clusters, published "Liveness Probes are Dangerous" in September 2019, adapted from Zalando's internal developer documentation. The post's opening point is that a wrong liveness probe "can worsen high-load situations (cascading failure + potential long container/app start)" and that "a Liveness Probe in combination with an external DB health check dependency is the worst situation: a single DB hiccup will restart all your containers!" It walks through the defaults (period 10 s, timeout 1 s, failure threshold 3), recommends always defining a readiness probe for HTTP services, warns against liveness probes that check dependencies or share an overloaded thread pool with request handling, and against probes on a separate management port that stays healthy while the main port is broken. Its conclusion is not "never use liveness probes" but "use them only with a clear use case and an understanding of the consequences".

Jacobs and colleagues also started Kubernetes Failure Stories (k8s.af), a curated list of public incident write-ups from many companies: DNS and ndots latency, CPU limits and throttling, OOM kills, etcd and API-server overload, admission webhooks blocking clusters, autoscaling surprises, cloud integration failures. Reading through it is the fastest way to learn which failure modes recur in practice; nearly every entry maps onto a mechanism in this track, and most were diagnosed with exactly the commands in this lesson. The meta-lesson the collection makes is that Kubernetes incidents are rarely exotic: they come from defaults left unexamined (probe timeouts, DNS settings, limits) interacting with load.

A triage runbook

  1. Scope: one pod, one Deployment, one node, one namespace or everything? kubectl get pods -A | grep -v Running, node status, recent changes (deploys, config, cluster upgrades).
  2. If a deploy just happened and users are affected: kubectl rollout undo (or revert in Git), then investigate.
  3. Describe one failing pod; identify the first stage that failed (primer figure).
  4. Read Last State and logs --previous; decode the exit code.
  5. For Pending or ContainerCreating, read events; for Ready-but-failing, walk endpoints → pod → Service → DNS → policy → entry point.
  6. Capture evidence (describe output, logs, events) before restarting or deleting anything.
  7. After the fix, write down what the evidence said and what alert would have caught it sooner.

Common traps during response

Restarting everything (kubectl rollout restart) as a first move hides the evidence and, in a liveness cascade or an overloaded dependency, restarts the cascade. Scaling up a service whose bottleneck is a database adds load to the database. Force-deleting stuck pods risks two writers on one volume. Editing live objects in a GitOps-managed cluster gets reverted within minutes (k8s12). The safe defaults are: capture evidence, roll back the last change, then debug.

Signals worth alerting on

Containers restarting more than N times in M minutes; pods in CrashLoopBackOff, ImagePullBackOff or CreateContainerConfigError for more than a few minutes; OOM kills (kube_pod_container_status_last_terminated_reason{reason="OOMKilled"}); pods Pending longer than the expected scale-up time; Deployments whose available replicas are below desired for minutes; readiness failures across many pods of one service at once (a dependency problem); nodes NotReady or under pressure.
myths: CrashLoopBackOff is an error type.

It is a waiting state: the container has exited repeatedly and the kubelet is waiting an increasing delay before starting it again. The actual error is in the previous run — its exit code and reason in Last State, and its logs, which you get with kubectl logs --previous.
kubectl logs shows why a container crashed.

kubectl logs shows the current container instance, which in a crash loop is often a fresh start with little or nothing logged. The crashed instance's output is under --previous. And if the process was killed by the kernel (OOMKilled) or by the kubelet (liveness failure), the application may have logged nothing at all; the reason is in describe.
Exit code 137 means out of memory.

137 means the process was killed by SIGKILL (128 + 9). The OOM killer is one sender; another is the kubelet sending SIGKILL after the grace period when a liveness probe failed or the pod was deleted and the process ignored SIGTERM. Check the termination reason (OOMKilled versus Error) and the events.
A failing liveness probe means the app is broken, so restarting helps.

Liveness probes often fail because the app is overloaded (slow responses exceed the 1-second default timeout) or because the probe checks a dependency. Restarting then removes capacity and cold-starts caches exactly when load is highest, turning a slowdown into a cascading outage. Liveness should detect only unrecoverable states such as deadlocks.
If kubectl exec doesn't work, you can't debug the container.

Minimal and distroless images have no shell, but kubectl debug can add an ephemeral container with any tools image to the running pod, sharing its namespaces and, with --target, its process namespace; kubectl debug --copy-to creates a modified copy; and kubectl debug node/<name> gives a shell with the node's file system at /host.
A pod that is Running is healthy.

Running only means the containers have been started and at least one is running. A pod can be Running but not Ready (failing its readiness probe, so it receives no traffic), restarting repeatedly, or ready but returning errors. Check READY, RESTARTS, conditions and the application's own metrics.
lab:
Steps 1-3 need a kind or minikube cluster; step 4 runs here with Python 3.12.

  1. Break it four ways (Needs a kind/minikube cluster). 
    kubectl run crash --image=busybox:1.37 -- sh -c 'echo starting; exit 3'
kubectl run oom --image=python:3.12-slim --overrides='{"spec":{"containers":[{"name":"oom","image":"python:3.12-slim","command":["python","-c","b=bytearray(300*1024*1024)"],"resources":{"limits":{"memory":"128Mi"}}}]}}'
