kubectl run cfg --image=busybox:1.37 --overrides='{"spec":{"containers":[{"name":"cfg","image":"busybox:1.37","command":["sleep","3600"],"env":[{"name":"X","valueFrom":{"secretKeyRef":{"name":"missing","key":"k"}}}]}]}}'
kubectl get pods -w
    Expect CrashLoopBackOff (exit code 3, logs --previous show "starting"), OOMKilled (exit 137), ImagePullBackOff (events: not found or denied), and CreateContainerConfigError (secret "missing" not found). Run kubectl describe pod on each and find the line that names the cause.
  2. A probe that kills (Needs a cluster). Deploy nginx:1.27 with a liveness probe on path /nope: events show Liveness probe failed: HTTP probe failed with statuscode: 404 and Container … failed liveness probe, will be restarted, and RESTARTS climbs every ~30 s. Change it to a readiness probe instead: the pod stays up, 0/1, with no restarts.
  3. Debug a shell-less container (Needs a cluster). kubectl run dl --image=gcr.io/distroless/static-debian12 --command -- /pause will fail (no such binary — exit 127 or StartError): note the reason. Then run any distroless app image and attach with kubectl debug -it pod/<name> --image=busybox:1.37 --target=<container>; run ps and ls /proc/1/root. Try kubectl debug node/kind-control-plane -it --image=busybox:1.37 and ls /host/var/log/pods.
  4. A describe-output triager (runs here). Save as triage.py: 
    import re
SIG = {137: "SIGKILL (OOM kill or killed after grace period)", 143: "SIGTERM (graceful stop)",
       139: "SIGSEGV (native crash)", 127: "command not found", 126: "command not executable",
       0: "exited successfully but restartPolicy wants it running"}
def triage(text):
    state = re.search(r"State:\s+(\w+)\s+Reason:\s+(\S+)", text)
    last = re.search(r"Last State:\s+Terminated\s+Reason:\s+(\S+)\s+Exit Code:\s+(\d+)", text)
    events = re.findall(r"(Warning|Normal)\s+(\w+)\s+.*?\s{2,}(\S+)\s{2,}(.*)", text)
    out = []
    if state: out.append(f"now: {state.group(1)} / {state.group(2)}")
    if last:
        reason, code = last.group(1), int(last.group(2))
        meaning = SIG.get(code, "application error" if code < 128 else f"killed by signal {code-128}")
        out.append(f"last run: {reason}, exit {code} = {meaning}")
        out.append("next: kubectl logs --previous" if reason == "Error" and code < 128 else
                   "next: check memory limit and memory.stat" if reason == "OOMKilled" else
                   "next: look for liveness/eviction/preemption events")
    for typ, reason, src, msg in events:
        if typ == "Warning": out.append(f"event {reason} from {src}: {msg.strip()}")
    return "\n".join(out)
sample = """    State:          Waiting
      Reason:       CrashLoopBackOff
    Last State:     Terminated
      Reason:       OOMKilled
      Exit Code:    137
Events:
  Warning  BackOff    2m (x26 over 12m)  kubelet  Back-off restarting failed container api"""
print(triage(sample))
    Expect it to report the waiting state, "OOMKilled, exit 137 = SIGKILL…", the memory hint and the BackOff event. Paste the real describe outputs from step 1 into sample and compare its verdicts with your own.
recap: Debugging follows the pod's life: is it scheduled (Pending), created (ContainerCreating), pulled (ImagePullBackOff), running and staying up (CrashLoopBackOff), ready (readiness), and serving correctly (Services, DNS, policy)?
kubectl describe pod shows the state, Last State with reason and exit code, restart count, conditions and recent events; kubectl get events and the controller's own describe fill in the rest.

Exit codes encode the cause: 1 or another small number is the application's own error, 126/127 a command that cannot run or is not found, 137 SIGKILL (OOM kill or forced termination), 139 a segmentation fault, 143 SIGTERM.
CrashLoopBackOff is the kubelet waiting before restarting a repeatedly failing container, starting at 10 seconds and doubling to a 5-minute cap, reset after 10 minutes of successful running.
ImagePullBackOff and ErrImagePull mean the image cannot be fetched: wrong name or tag, missing pull credentials, rate limits, registry unreachable or wrong architecture.
OOMKilled means the container exceeded its memory limit; read memory.stat in the cgroup or the container's memory metrics, and fix the leak, the limit or the workers.
Liveness probes restart containers and must test only the process's own ability to make progress; readiness probes gate traffic; startup probes protect slow starters.
kubectl logs --previous, kubectl debug with ephemeral containers, kubectl debug node, port-forward and the events stream are the core tools, and none require a shell in the image.
Pods stuck Terminating usually have finalizers waiting for a controller, or a node that is gone; force deletion skips safety checks and should be the last step, not the first.
glossary: CrashLoopBackOff
The waiting state of a container that keeps exiting; the kubelet delays each restart longer, up to five minutes.
CreateContainerConfigError
A waiting reason meaning the kubelet cannot build the container's configuration, typically a missing ConfigMap, Secret or key referenced by env.
ephemeral container
A temporary container added to a running pod with kubectl debug for troubleshooting; it cannot be removed or restarted and has no resources or probes.
ErrImagePull / ImagePullBackOff
Waiting reasons for a failed image pull and the back-off before retrying it.
event
A short-lived API object recording something a component did or observed (Scheduled, Pulled, BackOff, Unhealthy), retained for about an hour by default.
exit code
The number a process returns when it ends; 128 + N means it was killed by signal N.
finalizer
A key on an object's metadata that blocks its deletion until a controller removes it after cleanup.
Last State
The record in kubectl describe of a container's previous run: when it started and finished, its exit code and reason.
liveness probe
A periodic check whose repeated failure makes the kubelet restart the container.
port-forward
kubectl port-forward: a tunnel from a local port through the API server and kubelet to a port in a pod.
readiness probe
A periodic check whose failure removes the pod from Service endpoints without restarting it.
restart count
How many times a container in a pod has been restarted by the kubelet.
startup probe
A check that must succeed before liveness and readiness probes start, giving slow applications time to start.
termination message
A short message a container writes to /dev/termination-log (or the end of its logs) that appears in its terminated state.
drill:
Diagnose: every pod restarts during the evening peak

Every evening at about 19:00, all 30 pods of a Java API restart within two minutes, latency spikes and errors last ten minutes. Describe on a restarted pod shows Last State: Terminated, Reason: Error, Exit Code: 137, Restart Count: 1, and no OOMKilled. Container spec: limits: {cpu: "1", memory: 3Gi}, requests: {cpu: 500m, memory: 3Gi}; liveness probe httpGet /health on port 8080, default timing; /health runs SELECT 1 against Postgres and pings Redis. The database team reports a nightly report starting at 18:58 that makes queries slower for a few minutes. Explain the chain of events and fix it.

Answer

Chain: at 18:58 the report slows Postgres. /health runs a query, so its latency rises; the evening peak also pushes the 1-CPU limited JVM into CFS throttling (k8s10), slowing the health handler further. With the default timeoutSeconds: 1 and failureThreshold: 3, three consecutive slow responses within 30 seconds fail liveness on every pod at nearly the same time. The kubelet kills each container: SIGTERM, then SIGKILL after the grace period (exit 137, reason Error — not an OOM). All 30 JVMs restart together, with cold JIT and connection pools, under peak traffic, and their start-up queries hit the already slow database. Ten minutes of errors follow — a cascading failure caused by the health check, exactly the scenario Zalando's post describes.

Fix: make liveness check only the JVM's ability to respond (a trivial endpoint with no dependencies, served off the main request thread pool), with timeoutSeconds: 5 and failureThreshold: 6, or remove it; move the database and Redis checks into readiness so slow dependencies take pods out of rotation instead of killing them (and consider not failing readiness on every dependency blip, or every pod becomes unready together); add a startup probe for JVM warm-up; remove or raise the CPU limit to stop throttling; make the app exit cleanly on SIGTERM so restarts that do happen are graceful. Ask the database team to move the report to a replica. Verify by watching restarts and probe failure events during the next evening peak.
qa: E
A pod is in CrashLoopBackOff. What do you do first?

Run kubectl describe pod to see Last State — the reason, exit code and timestamps of the previous run — plus restart count and events. Then kubectl logs <pod> --previous (and -c for the right container) to see what the crashed instance printed. The exit code and logs together usually name the cause: a configuration error, a missing dependency, an OOM kill, or a liveness probe killing it.
E
What does ImagePullBackOff mean and what causes it?

The kubelet failed to pull the container image and is backing off before retrying. Causes: a typo in the image name or tag, a tag that does not exist, a private registry without imagePullSecrets or node credentials, registry rate limits, network or DNS problems reaching the registry, or no manifest for the node's architecture. The events in describe show the registry's error message.
E
What is the difference between a liveness and a readiness probe?

Readiness decides whether the pod receives traffic: when it fails, the pod is removed from Service endpoints but keeps running. Liveness decides whether the container is restarted: after failureThreshold consecutive failures (3 by default, every 10 seconds), the kubelet kills and restarts it. Startup probes delay both until a slow-starting app is up.
M
Exit code 137 — how do you tell an OOM kill from something else?

137 is SIGKILL. kubectl describe shows Last State Terminated with Reason: OOMKilled when the kernel killed it for exceeding its memory limit; Reason: Error with 137 means something else sent SIGKILL — usually the kubelet after the grace period, because a liveness probe failed or the pod was deleted and the process ignored SIGTERM. Events show 'Liveness probe failed… will be restarted' in the second case; node logs and memory.events in the cgroup confirm OOM kills.
M
A pod has been Pending for ten minutes. How do you debug it?

kubectl describe pod and read the FailedScheduling event: it lists, per reason, how many nodes were rejected — insufficient CPU or memory (requests too big or cluster full), untolerated taints, node affinity or topology spread unsatisfied, volume node affinity conflicts, unbound PVCs. If there is no event at all, the scheduler never saw it (scheduler down, or a schedulerName nobody serves). Then fix the request, add capacity, add tolerations, or fix the volume.
M
A pod is Running but 0/1 Ready. What do you check?

The readiness probe: describe shows 'Readiness probe failed' events with the HTTP status, timeout or command output. Check that the probe's port and path match what the app serves, that the timeout (1 second by default) is realistic, that the app has finished starting (use a startup probe), and whether readiness depends on a downstream that is failing. While not ready, the pod is excluded from Service endpoints.
M
How do you debug a container that has no shell?

kubectl debug -it <pod> --image=busybox --target=<container> adds an ephemeral container that shares the pod's network namespace and, with --target, the target container's process namespace, so ps shows its processes and /proc/<pid>/root exposes its file system. kubectl debug <pod> --copy-to=<new> --set-image=*=<debug-image> creates a modifiable copy. kubectl debug node/<node> runs a pod in the host namespaces with the node's file system at /host.
M
What causes CreateContainerConfigError?

The kubelet could not build the container's configuration before starting it: most often an env var or envFrom referencing a ConfigMap or Secret (or a key in one) that does not exist in the namespace, or an invalid security context such as runAsNonRoot with a non-numeric image user. describe shows the exact message, such as couldn't find key DATABASE_URL in Secret prod/db.
H
Explain how liveness probes can cause a cascading failure and how to design them safely.

If the liveness check depends on a database and the database slows, every pod's liveness fails, the kubelet restarts all of them, caches go cold and start-up load hits the struggling database, so the outage becomes total. The same happens under CPU saturation when a liveness endpoint misses its 1-second timeout. Safe design: liveness checks only that the process can make progress (a local endpoint, no dependencies), with generous timeouts and failure thresholds; readiness handles dependencies and overload by taking a pod out of rotation; startup probes cover slow starts; and many services need no liveness probe at all.

Follow-up: When is a liveness probe genuinely useful? — For applications that can deadlock or wedge without exiting, where a restart reliably fixes it, and where the probe can tell that state apart from slowness.
H
Pods of a Deployment are being killed every few hours with exit code 137 but no OOMKilled reason. What could it be?

Something sends SIGKILL other than the OOM killer. Candidates: liveness probe failures during load spikes (events say 'Liveness probe failed'); node-pressure eviction (the pod would show Evicted and be replaced); preemption by higher-priority pods (Preempted events); consolidation or node drains (Karpenter or autoscaler events) where the app ignores SIGTERM and is killed after the grace period. Correlate the timestamps of Last State with events, node events and autoscaler logs.
H
Walk through debugging 'the service returns 503 since the last deploy' from first command to fix.

kubectl get pods -l app=x: are new pods Ready and not restarting? If not ready, describe for readiness failures and logs. If ready, kubectl get endpointslices for the Service: are pod IPs listed with ready true, and does the Service's selector and targetPort match the new pods' labels and port (a renamed port or changed label is common)? Then from a debug pod, curl the pod IP directly and the Service name to split app, Service and DNS problems; check NetworkPolicy and the Gateway's route status. Roll back with kubectl rollout undo if users are affected while you investigate.
H
A namespace has been stuck in Terminating for an hour. Why, and how do you resolve it safely?

Namespace deletion waits until every object in it is deleted, and objects with finalizers wait for their controller to remove them. Typical blockers are custom resources whose operator was deleted first (so nobody removes their finalizer), or an unavailable aggregated API that prevents the namespace controller from listing resources. Find them with kubectl api-resources --namespaced -o name | xargs -n1 kubectl get -n <ns>, and the namespace's status conditions. Fix the cause — reinstall the operator or restore the API — and let cleanup run; only remove finalizers manually when you know the external cleanup they guard is unnecessary.

t: Kubernetes for ML: GPU scheduling, KServe, Ray on Kubernetes and model-serving autoscaling
sum: How a GPU reaches a container (driver, container toolkit, device plugin, nvidia.com/gpu), sharing GPUs with time-slicing, MPS and MIG, Dynamic Resource Allocation, gang scheduling and Kueue for training, cold starts of multi-gigabyte images and models worked by hand, KServe's standard and scale-to-zero modes, autoscaling inference on queue depth rather than GPU utilisation, and KubeRay — with OpenAI's 7,500-node cluster as the case.
prereq: gpu1
A GPU is a throughput machine of SMs, tensor cores and HBM; utilisation metrics can mislead, and memory capacity often decides what fits.
lm13
LLM serving is shaped by continuous batching, KV-cache memory and prefill/decode; time to first token and throughput depend on batch size and queueing.
ae8
ML systems move from training pipelines to registries to batch, online or streaming serving, with canary rollouts and monitoring.
k8s10
Requests drive scheduling, taints and tolerations reserve node pools, priority enables preemption, and DRA allocates structured devices.
k8s11
The HPA scales replicas on a metric ratio, KEDA scales on external signals and to zero, and node autoscalers add capacity for pending pods in minutes.
why:
An ML team moves its work onto the company's Kubernetes platform. Within a month, every lesson in this track shows up again, amplified by the price of a GPU. A data scientist's notebook pod holds an 80 GB H100 for a week while using it a few minutes a day. Two distributed training jobs each grab half the free GPUs and wait forever for the other half. A new LLM endpoint takes nine minutes to serve its first request after a scale-up, because a fresh GPU node must boot, pull a 9 GB serving image, download 16 GB of weights and load them into GPU memory. The autoscaler, configured on GPU utilisation, never scales: the GPUs read "98% utilised" while requests queue. And a training job that has run for eleven hours is OOM-killed by the container's memory limit — not GPU memory, host memory, eaten by data-loader workers.

None of these failures needs new Kubernetes concepts. They need the existing ones applied to hardware that is scarce, expensive, slow to provision and shaped differently from CPUs. A GPU is an integer resource that cannot be overcommitted. It reaches a container through a driver, a runtime hook and a device plugin rather than a cgroup. It can be split in software or in hardware, with very different isolation. Training jobs need all their workers at once. Serving replicas carry gigabytes of state that must be loaded before they help. And the most-quoted GPU metric does not mean what people think (gpu1).

This lesson connects the Kubernetes mechanics of k8s1-k8s13 to ML workloads. It starts with how a GPU gets into a container and how the scheduler accounts for it, then sharing GPUs with time-slicing, MPS and MIG, and the newer Dynamic Resource Allocation. It covers training — gang scheduling and quota queues with Kueue — then serving: cold starts worked out with real image and model sizes, keeping weights out of images, KServe's two deployment modes, and autoscaling inference on signals that track load (lm13's queues and KV-cache). It closes with Ray on Kubernetes and with OpenAI's account of running training clusters of 7,500 nodes.
primer:
Specialist ovens in a shared kitchen

Picture a commercial kitchen. Most work uses the ordinary hobs and counters, which are shared flexibly: a cook can use a bit more counter space when nobody else needs it (CPU and memory, k8s10). But a few stations have a specialist oven that costs as much as the rest of the kitchen put together. Ovens are booked whole — you cannot book half an oven — and the booking sheet only counts ovens, not how hot each one is running.

  • Getting an oven needs three things on that station: the oven's own wiring (the GPU driver on the node), an adapter that lets a cook's equipment plug into it (the NVIDIA Container Toolkit), and a sign on the station listing how many ovens it has (the device plugin, which tells the kubelet "this node has 8 nvidia.com/gpu"). The GPU Operator is the contractor who installs and maintains all three.
  • Sharing an oven: you can let several cooks take turns (time-slicing), let them use it at once and hope they don't clash (MPS), or install fixed internal walls so it becomes several smaller, isolated ovens (MIG).
  • Banquets (distributed training) need all their ovens at the same moment; booking half and waiting for the rest wastes the half. A maître d' with a reservation book (Kueue) only seats a banquet when all its ovens are free.
  • Restaurants (model serving) must preheat: a new oven is useless until it is installed, the right equipment is fetched and the dish is prepared. Keeping some ovens warm, and the ingredients nearby, is what makes service fast.

Three workload shapes, three sets of rules

ML on Kubernetes is really three workload shapes with different needs. Interactive work (notebooks, experiments) holds resources for long periods while using them in bursts; it needs cheap, shareable GPUs and automatic clean-up. Training runs for hours or days on many GPUs at once; it needs all of them together, fast interconnect between them, fair sharing between teams, and protection from interruption or the ability to resume after it. Serving runs indefinitely with traffic that rises and falls; it needs fast start-up, autoscaling on the right signal and isolation from noisy neighbours. Most of the mistakes in the opening story come from applying one shape's rules to another — serving-style Deployments for training, training-style whole-GPU allocations for notebooks, CPU-style autoscaling for inference.

Where the analogy breaks: an oven's heat is a fair measure of its work, but a GPU's "utilisation" number is not. It reports the fraction of time any kernel was running, so a GPU doing light work continuously looks as busy as one running flat out (gpu1). Decisions about capacity need better signals, from the serving engine or from finer-grained GPU counters.
body:
1. How a GPU reaches a container

Containers get CPU and memory through cgroups (k8s10). A GPU is different: it is a PCIe device driven by a kernel driver, used by applications through user-space libraries (libcuda, NVML) that must match the driver version. Four pieces make it work on Kubernetes:

  1. The driver on the host creates device files (/dev/nvidia0 … /dev/nvidia7, /dev/nvidiactl, /dev/nvidia-uvm) and loads the kernel modules.
  2. The NVIDIA Container Toolkit integrates with containerd or CRI-O so that, when a container is created with certain GPUs assigned, the runtime adds those device files and bind-mounts the matching driver libraries and utilities into the container (today usually through the Container Device Interface, CDI, a standard for describing such device injections). The image therefore does not contain the driver — only CUDA user-space libraries that must be compatible with it.
  3. The device plugin runs as a DaemonSet and talks to the kubelet's device plugin API over a Unix socket: it registers the resource name nvidia.com/gpu, streams the list of healthy devices (ListAndWatch), and, when the kubelet starts a container that was allocated GPUs, answers Allocate with what the runtime must inject for those specific device IDs. The kubelet adds the count to the node's capacity and allocatable, so kubectl describe node shows nvidia.com/gpu: 8.
  4. The GPU Operator installs and manages these as Kubernetes components: the driver (as a container), toolkit, device plugin, GPU feature discovery (which labels nodes with nvidia.com/gpu.product=NVIDIA-H100-80GB-HBM3, memory, count and MIG capability), the DCGM exporter (metrics and health) and the MIG manager — all reconciled from one custom resource, so versions stay consistent across nodes.

A pod asks for GPUs as an extended resource:

resources:
  limits:
    nvidia.com/gpu: 1        # whole GPUs; requests, if set, must equal limits
    cpu: "8"
    memory: 64Gi
nodeSelector:
  nvidia.com/gpu.product: NVIDIA-H100-80GB-HBM3
tolerations:
- { key: nvidia.com/gpu, operator: Exists, effect: NoSchedule }

The rules from the Kubernetes docs: GPUs are specified in limits; requests default to the limit and must equal it if given; you cannot specify requests without limits; and the quantity is an integer. The scheduler counts GPUs exactly like CPU against allocatable (k8s6), but there is no overcommit and no sharing: a pod that gets one GPU has it exclusively, whether it uses it fully or not. The node selector picks a GPU model; the toleration lets the pod onto GPU nodes that are tainted to keep everything else off (k8s10). Many managed platforms add the taint to GPU node pools and the toleration to GPU-requesting pods automatically.

2. Sharing a GPU: time-slicing, MPS and MIG

Whole-GPU allocation wastes money for small workloads: a 7B-parameter model in 4-bit weights, a notebook, a small embedding service might need 10 GB and a fraction of the compute of an 80 GB H100. There are three ways to share, configured at the node level and surfaced to pods as resources.

Time-slicingMPSMIG
HowProcesses take turns on the whole GPUOne server process runs several clients' kernels concurrentlyHardware partitions with dedicated SMs, memory and cache
Memory isolationNone: all share all memoryLimited (per-client limits possible)Full
Fault isolationNoneLimited (a fault can affect all clients)Full
PerformanceContext switching; noisy neighboursGood for many small kernelsPredictable per slice
HardwareAny NVIDIA GPUVolta and laterA100, H100 and later data-centre GPUs
Exposed asnvidia.com/gpu × replicas (or renamed .shared)Same, via MPS sharing confige.g. nvidia.com/mig-1g.10gb

Time-slicing is a device-plugin setting: "advertise each GPU as 4". A node with 8 GPUs then shows nvidia.com/gpu: 32, and up to four pods share each GPU by time. Nothing stops one of them from allocating all 80 GB, crashing the others with out-of-memory errors, so it suits development, notebooks and light inference where tenants trust each other. MPS lets kernels from several processes run at the same time rather than in turns, improving throughput for many small kernels, with partial isolation.

MIG (Multi-Instance GPU) splits a supported GPU in hardware. An H100 80GB can be partitioned, for example, into seven 1g.10gb instances (each one-seventh of the compute with 10 GB), or into mixes such as 3g.40gb + 2g.20gb + 1g.10gb; each instance has its own memory, cache and SMs, so a fault or memory exhaustion in one does not affect the others. With the device plugin's mixed strategy, each profile is its own resource, and a pod asks for nvidia.com/mig-1g.10gb: 1. The MIG manager applies a node's partition layout from a label. The trade-off is rigidity: slice sizes are fixed per GPU model, re-partitioning requires draining the GPU, and a workload that needs 15 GB must take a 20 GB slice.

3. Dynamic Resource Allocation

Counting identical devices works for "one GPU". It struggles with "a GPU with at least 40 GB of memory and compute capability 9.0, on the same NVLink domain as another", or "a 2g.20gb MIG slice created on demand". Dynamic Resource Allocation (DRA), which the Kubernetes documentation lists as stable since 1.35, replaces counted resources with claims. A driver publishes ResourceSlices describing each node's devices and their attributes; administrators define DeviceClasses; a pod references a ResourceClaim (or a template that creates one per pod) whose requests select devices with CEL expressions on attributes:

apiVersion: resource.k8s.io/v1
kind: ResourceClaimTemplate
metadata: { name: big-gpu }
spec:
  spec:
    devices:
      requests:
      - name: gpu
        exactly:
          deviceClassName: gpu.nvidia.com
          selectors:
          - cel: { expression: "device.capacity['gpu.nvidia.com'].memory.compareTo(quantity('40Gi')) >= 0" }

The scheduler allocates matching devices as part of placement, and the driver prepares them on the node. DRA is how structured sharing, partitioning on demand and device topology are being brought into the scheduler rather than bolted on beside it; NVIDIA publishes a DRA driver for GPUs. For most clusters today, the device-plugin resources above remain the common path, and DRA is worth adopting where its selection power is needed.

4. Training: gang scheduling and quota queues

A distributed data-parallel training job — say 4 nodes × 8 GPUs with PyTorch's distributed launcher, or an MPI job — only makes progress when every worker is running, because each step synchronises gradients across all of them. Kubernetes' default scheduler places one pod at a time (k8s6), and that creates a classic deadlock. Worked example: a cluster has 16 free GPUs on two 8-GPU nodes. Job A and job B are each 4 pods × 4 GPUs (16 GPUs). Their pods are created at the same moment and interleave in the scheduling queue: A-0 and B-0 land on node 1, A-1 and B-1 on node 2. All 16 GPUs are now allocated; A-2, A-3, B-2 and B-3 are Pending. Neither job can start, and neither will release its GPUs — they are waiting on each other forever, while the GPUs sit idle and bill.

The fix is gang scheduling: admit all of a job's pods, or none. The most common way in Kubernetes is Kueue, a SIG Scheduling project that works with standard Jobs, JobSets, Kubeflow training jobs, RayJobs and more:

  • Jobs are created suspended (spec.suspend: true, k8s7) and placed in a LocalQueue for their namespace, pointing at a ClusterQueue that holds quota per ResourceFlavor (for example 64 H100s and 32 L4s).
  • Kueue admits a job only when its whole request fits in the queue's available quota, then unsuspends it, so all its pods are created together and fit. In the example, A is admitted (16 GPUs), B waits in the queue, and A runs.
  • ClusterQueues in a cohort can borrow each other's unused quota and reclaim it by preemption, so a research team can use idle production-reserved GPUs at night and give them back in the morning; fair sharing balances usage across teams over time.

Alternatives include the scheduler's coscheduling plugin (pods labelled into a PodGroup with a minimum member count), and batch schedulers such as Volcano. Placement also matters: workers that exchange gradients every step should sit on nodes with fast interconnect between them, so training platforms add topology labels (rack, network block) and topology-aware scheduling, and multi-node jobs often use JobSet or LeaderWorkerSet to manage groups of pods as one unit. Finally, long jobs must survive disruption: checkpoint regularly to object storage (k8s9), protect running jobs from consolidation and drains (karpenter.sh/do-not-disrupt, k8s11), and make restarts resume from the last checkpoint.

5. Serving: where a cold start goes

A model server replica is not ready until it has the model in GPU memory, so its start-up is much longer than a web service's. Work through a new replica of an 8B-parameter LLM served with vLLM, scheduled when no GPU node has room:

StepSize or workCold nodeWarm node, cached
Provision GPU node, boot, join, GPU stack readyVM + driver + device plugin~2-4 min0
Pull serving imagevllm/vllm-openai ≈ 8.7 GB compressed~45-90 s at 100-200 MB/s, plus unpack0 (present)
Fetch weights8B × 2 bytes (BF16) ≈ 16 GB16 s at 1 GB/s; 80 s at 200 MB/s0 (node cache)
Load to GPU, warm up engineCopy 16 GB to HBM, allocate KV cache, capture graphs~20-60 s~20-60 s
Total to Ready~4-7 min~0.5-1 min

The image size is real: the vllm/vllm-openai image on Docker Hub is about 8.7 GB compressed for amd64, and even a minimal pytorch/pytorch CUDA runtime image is about 3.3 GB (the devel variant, with compilers, about 14 GB). A 70B model in BF16 is about 140 GB of weights, which changes "seconds" into "minutes" at any realistic bandwidth. The table shows where to attack:

  • Keep weights out of the image. Images change rarely, weights often; baking them together makes every model update a huge push and every pull a huge download. Store weights in object storage or a model registry (ae8) and fetch them at start.
  • Cache weights per node, not per pod. Download once to node-local NVMe (a DaemonSet or init container populating a hostPath or local volume), or a shared read-many volume (k8s9), so the second replica on a node starts from local disk. Image volumes (stable since 1.36) mount an OCI image or artefact read-only into a pod: package weights as an OCI artefact, store it in your registry next to the serving image, and let the node's image cache and pull machinery (and signing, k8s5) handle it.
  • Pre-pull serving images into GPU node images, or with a DaemonSet, and use lazy-loading snapshotters for the remainder (k8s1).
  • Keep warm capacity: placeholder pods on GPU nodes (k8s11's overprovisioning) or a minimum replica count, so scale-up lands on a ready node.
  • Use startup probes sized to the real load time, so the liveness probe does not kill a replica that is still loading (k8s13), and readiness that passes only when the model is loaded.

6. KServe: InferenceService and its two modes

KServe is a Kubernetes-native model-serving platform. You describe the model, not the Deployment:

apiVersion: serving.kserve.io/v1beta1
kind: InferenceService
metadata: { name: summariser }
spec:
  predictor:
    minReplicas: 1
    maxReplicas: 8
    model:
      modelFormat: { name: huggingface }
      storageUri: s3://models/summariser/v7
      resources:
        limits: { nvidia.com/gpu: 1, cpu: "8", memory: 48Gi }

KServe picks a serving runtime for the model format (for LLMs typically vLLM-based), runs a storage initializer that downloads storageUri into the pod before the server starts, and creates the routing. It supports canary rollouts between model versions and, for LLMs, an LLMInferenceService resource with features such as disaggregated prefill and decode. It has two deployment modes:

  • Standard mode (previously called raw deployment) creates ordinary Deployments and Services, scaled by an HPA or KEDA. KServe's documentation recommends it for most production scenarios and especially for LLM serving: predictable scaling, standard networking, no extra dependencies.
  • Knative mode runs the predictor as a Knative Service. Knative's autoscaler scales on request concurrency: with a target of, say, 4 concurrent requests per replica and 37 requests in flight, it wants ceil(37 ÷ 4) = 10 replicas. It can scale to zero after a period without traffic; the next request is held by Knative's activator, which triggers scale-from-zero and forwards the request once a replica is ready. That is ideal for many rarely used models on shared GPUs, and a cold start of the length worked above for the unlucky first caller.

7. Autoscaling inference on the right signal

For CPU services, CPU utilisation is a usable proxy for load. For GPU inference, the obvious analogue — GPU utilisation — is misleading. The commonly exported DCGM utilisation metric (DCGM_FI_DEV_GPU_UTIL) measures the fraction of time in the sample period that at least one kernel was executing (gpu1). An LLM server doing continuous batching runs decode kernels almost constantly, so it reads close to 100% at modest load and stays there as load doubles; meanwhile the real limits — KV-cache memory and batch slots (lm13) — determine when requests start to queue.

Better signals come from the serving engine itself. vLLM, for example, exports Prometheus metrics for requests running and requests waiting, and KV-cache usage. A KEDA ScaledObject (k8s11) on waiting requests:

triggers:
- type: prometheus
  metadata:
    serverAddress: http://prometheus.monitoring:9090
    query: sum(vllm:num_requests_waiting{model_name="summariser"})
    threshold: "4"          # target: about 4 waiting requests per replica

Worked: 3 replicas, 26 requests waiting → the HPA KEDA manages computes ceil(26 ÷ 4) = 7 replicas; as the queue drains, the scale-down window holds capacity before releasing it. Pair this with: a scale-down stabilization window of many minutes (replicas are slow to start, so flapping is expensive); a minReplicas that covers baseline traffic; warm GPU capacity for the first scale-up step; and a router that spreads requests well — long-lived connections and very uneven request sizes defeat per-connection balancing (k8s8), which is why inference-aware gateways route by queue length or prefix-cache affinity.

8. Ray on Kubernetes with KubeRay

Ray is a Python framework for distributed computing — data processing (Ray Data), training (Ray Train), tuning and serving (Ray Serve) — with its own scheduler for tasks and actors inside a cluster of processes. KubeRay is the operator that runs Ray clusters on Kubernetes:

  • RayCluster: a head pod (cluster control, the Global Control Service) and one or more worker groups, each a pod template with resources — for example a CPU group for preprocessing and a GPU group for training — with min and max replicas.
  • RayJob: submits a job to a RayCluster (creating one if needed) and can tear it down when the job finishes; works with Kueue for gang admission.
  • RayService: runs Ray Serve applications with zero-downtime upgrades of the underlying cluster.

Scaling is layered exactly as in k8s11: when Ray tasks or actors need more resources than the cluster has, the Ray autoscaler asks KubeRay for more worker pods; pending worker pods make Karpenter or the Cluster Autoscaler add GPU nodes. Ray suits workloads that are naturally Python-level graphs of tasks — a pipeline that reads data, tokenises on CPUs and embeds on GPUs, or hyperparameter search over hundreds of trials — that would be clumsy as many separate Kubernetes Jobs.

9. Observing GPU workloads

Because the headline utilisation number misleads (section 7), GPU observability needs a few more signals. The DCGM exporter publishes per-GPU metrics labelled with the pod that holds the GPU, so they join cleanly with Kubernetes data. Device-level fields include memory in use (DCGM_FI_DEV_FB_USED), temperature, power and clock throttling, and XID error counts (DCGM_FI_DEV_XID_ERRORS) for health. The profiling fields are the ones that describe how busy the GPU really is: DCGM_FI_PROF_SM_ACTIVE (the fraction of time streaming multiprocessors have work), DCGM_FI_PROF_SM_OCCUPANCY (how full they are), DCGM_FI_PROF_PIPE_TENSOR_ACTIVE (tensor-core use) and DCGM_FI_PROF_DRAM_ACTIVE (memory-bandwidth use). A training job that shows 99% utilisation but 30% tensor activity and high DRAM activity is memory-bound (gpu1); an inference server with low SM activity and a growing request queue is limited elsewhere — the CPU, the network or the batch configuration.

Join these with the application's own metrics — step time and tokens per second for training, waiting requests, time to first token and time per output token for serving (lm13) — and with Kubernetes data: pods per GPU node, pending GPU pods, Kueue admission and wait times, and cold-start durations. The questions a platform team must answer every week are "which teams hold GPUs they are not using?", "which jobs wait longest and why?" and "how long does a new replica take to serve?"; each needs at least one metric from each of the three layers.
deep:
GPU health is a first-class scheduling concern

At fleet scale, GPUs fail in ways CPUs rarely do: uncorrectable memory errors, a GPU "falling off the bus", NVLink errors, thermal throttling. The driver reports many of them as XID errors in the kernel log; DCGM exposes health checks and counters. A failed GPU on an 8-GPU node can stall a 512-GPU training job, so platforms automate detection and response: the device plugin marks unhealthy devices so they are no longer allocatable; node health agents read XIDs and DCGM diagnostics and taint or cordon the node; active tests run when a node joins (and periodically) before the taint that keeps workloads off is removed; and remediation resets GPUs, reboots or replaces the VM. OpenAI's case below describes exactly this split between passive and active checks.

Topology and interconnect

Within a node, GPUs connected by NVLink and NVSwitch exchange data an order of magnitude faster than over PCIe; across nodes, training traffic uses high-bandwidth fabrics such as InfiniBand or RoCE with RDMA, often through dedicated network interfaces attached to pods (SR-IOV, multi-network). Kubernetes' kubelet has a Topology Manager that aligns CPUs, memory and devices on the same NUMA node for a pod, and schedulers and Kueue can use node labels for network topology to keep a job's workers in the same block. For an 8-GPU pod the question is mostly solved by taking the whole node; for jobs spanning many nodes, placement within the network topology can change step time noticeably, which is why large training clusters are scheduled with topology awareness rather than as a flat pool.

The economics of idle GPUs

A GPU's hourly price is roughly that of dozens of CPU cores, so the waste patterns of k8s10 — inflated requests, idle reservations — cost an order of magnitude more. Common leaks: notebooks holding whole GPUs for days (cull idle notebooks, or give them time-sliced or MIG slices); inference replicas sized for peak all day (autoscale on queue depth with warm minimums rather than fixed fleets); training jobs that crash at hour ten and restart from zero (checkpoint); and GPUs blocked by deadlocked partial gangs (Kueue). Spot GPUs cut prices substantially for checkpointed training and for inference with enough replicas to absorb interruptions. The metric to watch is not "GPU utilisation" but allocated-versus-busy GPU hours per team, from Kueue and DCGM together.

Multi-node inference

Models too large for one node's GPUs (hundreds of billions of parameters) are served across several nodes with tensor and pipeline parallelism. Each replica is then a group of pods that must start together, share a leader for coordination and be replaced together: LeaderWorkerSet provides that unit, with gang-like semantics for groups and rolling updates of whole groups. Autoscaling then adds or removes whole groups, each costing a large multi-node allocation, which makes warm capacity and accurate queue-based signals even more important.

Batch inference as a cheaper path

Not every model call needs an online endpoint. Scoring a table of a million rows overnight, embedding a document corpus or running evaluation suites are throughput problems, not latency problems (ae8). On Kubernetes they fit Indexed Jobs or RayJobs (k8s7) admitted through Kueue, running at large batch sizes on spot or borrowed GPUs, with checkpointed progress per shard. Moving work from always-on endpoints to scheduled batch jobs is often the single largest cost reduction available to an ML platform, because it turns idle reserved capacity into fully used, interruptible capacity.

Driver and CUDA compatibility

The driver lives on the node; CUDA libraries live in images. NVIDIA's compatibility rules let newer drivers run images built against older CUDA versions, and within a major CUDA version, images built for a newer minor version can often run on an older driver with limitations. Practically: pin a driver branch per node pool, test images against it in CI, and upgrade drivers through the GPU Operator node by node (it drains GPU pods first). A mismatch shows up as "CUDA driver version is insufficient for CUDA runtime version" at start-up — an error that is about the node, not the image.

Inference routing that understands models

Generic load balancing treats every request as equal, but LLM requests differ by orders of magnitude in prompt and output length, and replicas differ in what they have cached. Model-aware routing — for example the Gateway API Inference Extension, which lets a Gateway pick an endpoint using signals such as each replica's queue length and KV-cache usage, or routing that prefers the replica already holding a conversation's prefix in its cache (lm13's prefix caching) — reduces tail latency and wasted recomputation, and it changes autoscaling too, because a fleet with balanced queues saturates evenly rather than one replica at a time. It is the inference-specific answer to the per-connection balancing problem of k8s8, and it is moving quickly, so check what your Gateway implementation and serving engine support before designing around a specific feature.

The case: OpenAI, "Scaling Kubernetes to 7,500 nodes" (January 2021)

OpenAI described how it ran Kubernetes clusters of up to 7,500 nodes for research workloads behind models such as GPT-3, CLIP and DALL·E, following an earlier post about 2,500 nodes. Its workload is unusual for Kubernetes and typical of large-scale ML: a pod usually takes a whole node, so the scheduler is rarely bin-packing; large jobs span many nodes and communicate with MPI, over SSH between pods' IPs rather than through Services; and a failing worker can force the whole job to restart from a checkpoint, so reliability of every node matters more than load balancing.

The post maps onto this track almost section by section. Networking: Flannel's overlay could not keep up at that scale, so they moved to the cloud's native pod networking with routable pod IPs (k8s8), and used iptables mangle rules with an exporter to account for internet-bound versus internal traffic. Control plane: API servers and etcd on dedicated nodes, with events stored in a separate etcd cluster to protect the main one, and attention to the load from watches and EndpointSlices (k8s6). Monitoring: Prometheus hit memory and crash problems with their metric volume and needed tuning. Health checks: passive checks continuously watching network, disk and GPU errors (including XIDs) to cordon or drain bad nodes, and active GPU tests at boot and periodically, with nodes kept tainted until they pass — the "GPU health is a scheduling concern" pattern above. Quotas: a team-resource-manager that applied team taints so nodes were reserved per team, with tolerations on that team's pods (k8s10). Autoscaling: CPU and GPU "balloon" Deployments of low-priority pods kept the cluster autoscaler from removing idle capacity, the overprovisioning pattern of k8s11. Gang scheduling: they adopted the scheduler's Coscheduling plugin so jobs' pods start together.

The lesson is not that every ML platform should run 7,500-node clusters, but that ML on Kubernetes works by applying ordinary Kubernetes mechanisms deliberately — taints, priorities, gang admission, overprovisioning, health-driven cordoning — to scarce, failure-prone hardware, and by simplifying where the workload allows (one pod per node, no service mesh for training).

Failure modes on GPU platforms

  • Pending: Insufficient nvidia.com/gpu: no free GPUs, or the device plugin is not running on new nodes (allocatable shows 0); check the GPU Operator's pods on the node.
  • "CUDA driver version is insufficient" or no CUDA-capable device: driver/image mismatch, or the pod did not request a GPU and therefore received none.
  • Partial gangs holding GPUs: training without Kueue or coscheduling.
  • Time-sliced tenants crashing each other with out-of-memory errors: move to MIG or dedicated GPUs.
  • Slow scale-up, then latency SLO breach: cold starts dominated by node provisioning, image pull and weight download.
  • Host OOM kills in training: data-loader workers and /dev/shm (k8s10, k8s13).
  • Silent GPU degradation: XID errors, throttling or ECC errors slowing a whole job; watch DCGM and step time.

What to measure

GPUs allocated versus busy per team (Kueue admission plus DCGM), queue wait time for training jobs, preemptions and restarts, cold-start time from pod creation to Ready for serving replicas, waiting requests and time to first token per model (lm13), and node health events.

Capacity planning for GPUs

Because GPU nodes are slow and sometimes impossible to obtain on demand, capacity is planned rather than purely autoscaled: reserved or committed capacity for steady serving and scheduled training, on-demand for daily peaks, spot for interruptible batch work, and a forecast reviewed monthly against queue wait times. Treat "GPU unavailable in this zone" as a normal event the platform handles — by falling back to other zones, instance types or queues — rather than as an outage.
myths: A pod can request half a GPU with nvidia.com/gpu: 0.5.

Extended resources such as nvidia.com/gpu are whole integers and cannot be overcommitted; limits must be set and requests, if given, must equal them. Sharing a GPU needs a deliberate mechanism: time-slicing or MPS configured in the device plugin (which advertises several 'replicas' per physical GPU), MIG partitions that appear as separate resources, or Dynamic Resource Allocation.
Time-slicing a GPU between pods isolates them like MIG does.

Time-slicing only interleaves processes in time; all of them share the full GPU memory with no limits, so one pod can exhaust memory and crash the others, and a noisy pod slows its neighbours. MIG partitions memory, cache and compute in hardware, giving each slice predictable performance and fault isolation, at the cost of fixed slice sizes.
GPU utilisation is the right metric for autoscaling inference.

The common DCGM utilisation metric reports the fraction of time any kernel was running, not how much of the GPU was busy. A server running small, memory-bound decode kernels can show near 100% while having plenty of headroom, or low values while requests queue on the CPU side. Queue depth, in-flight requests or KV-cache usage from the serving engine track user-facing load far better.
Kubernetes' default scheduler is fine for distributed training.

The default scheduler places pods one at a time. Two 8-GPU training jobs on a cluster with 8 free GPUs can each get 4 pods running and 4 pending, holding GPUs forever while neither can start. Distributed training needs gang (all-or-nothing) admission, provided by Kueue, the coscheduling plugin or schedulers such as Volcano, plus topology-aware placement.
Baking model weights into the container image makes serving simpler.

It makes every model change a multi-gigabyte image build and push, and every new replica on a cold node pull the weights through the image path before it can start. Weights belong in object storage, a shared or node-local cache, or an OCI artefact mounted as an image volume, so images stay stable and weights are fetched once per node.
Scale-to-zero is free money for GPU inference.

It saves the cost of idle GPUs but the first request after idling waits for a pod to be scheduled, possibly a GPU node to be provisioned, a large image to be pulled and a model to be loaded into GPU memory: tens of seconds to many minutes. It suits rarely used or internal models with relaxed latency, not latency-sensitive production endpoints.

Steps 1-2 need a Kubernetes cluster with NVIDIA GPUs (kind and minikube without GPUs cannot run them; minikube's Docker driver can pass GPUs through on an NVIDIA Linux host with minikube start --gpus all). Step 3 runs here with Python 3.12.

  1. See the GPU resource (Needs a GPU cluster). 
    kubectl describe node <gpu-node> | grep -A8 -E 'Capacity|Allocatable'   # nvidia.com/gpu: 1 or more
kubectl get nodes -L nvidia.com/gpu.product,nvidia.com/gpu.memory
kubectl apply -f - <<'EOF'
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata: { name: gpu-test }
spec:
  restartPolicy: Never
  containers:
  - name: cuda
    image: nvcr.io/nvidia/cuda:12.6.3-base-ubuntu24.04
    command: ["nvidia-smi", "-L"]
    resources: { limits: { nvidia.com/gpu: 1 } }
EOF
kubectl logs gpu-test        # GPU 0: NVIDIA … (UUID: GPU-…)
    Remove the limits and run again: nvidia-smi fails — a container gets no GPU unless it asks.
  2. Time-slicing (Needs a GPU cluster with the GPU Operator). Apply a device-plugin config with sharing.timeSlicing.resources: [{name: nvidia.com/gpu, replicas: 4}] as in the GPU Operator docs, label the node to use it, and watch allocatable become 4× the GPU count. Run four gpu-test-style pods sleeping on one GPU; nvidia-smi in each shows the same physical GPU and the others' processes.
  3. Gangs, queues and cold starts (runs here). Save as mlplatform.py: 
    import math
def place(jobs, nodes, gang):
    free = dict(nodes); placed = {j: 0 for j, _, _ in jobs}
    if gang:                                       # admit whole jobs only
        for name, pods, gpus in jobs:
            fits, trial = 0, dict(free)
            for _ in range(pods):
                n = next((k for k, v in trial.items() if v >= gpus), None)
                if n is None: break
                trial[n] -= gpus; fits += 1
            if fits == pods: free, placed[name] = trial, pods
    else:                                          # one pod at a time, interleaved
        for i in range(max(p for _, p, _ in jobs)):
            for name, pods, gpus in jobs:
                if i < pods:
                    n = next((k for k, v in free.items() if v >= gpus), None)
                    if n: free[n] -= gpus; placed[name] += 1
    return {j: f"{placed[j]}/{p} pods" for j, p, _ in jobs}
jobs = [("A", 4, 4), ("B", 4, 4)]                 # 4 pods x 4 GPUs each
nodes = {"node1": 8, "node2": 8}
print("default scheduler:", place(jobs, nodes, gang=False))
print("gang admission:   ", place(jobs, nodes, gang=True))
def cold_start(image_gb=8.7, weights_gb=16, net_gbps=0.2, node_min=3, load_s=40, warm=False):
    t = load_s + (0 if warm else node_min * 60 + image_gb / net_gbps + weights_gb / net_gbps)
    return round(t / 60, 1)
print("cold start (min):", cold_start(), " warm node:", cold_start(warm=True))
print("70B BF16 weights on cold node:", cold_start(weights_gb=140))
for waiting in (0, 6, 26, 80):
    print(waiting, "waiting ->", max(1, math.ceil(waiting / 4)), "replicas (target 4, min 1)")
    Expect the default scheduler to give both jobs 2/4 pods (deadlock, all 16 GPUs held) and gang admission to give A 4/4 and B 0/4 (queued); a cold start of roughly 5 minutes versus under a minute warm, and around 15 minutes for 140 GB of weights at 200 MB/s; and 1, 2, 7, 20 replicas for the queue values.
recap: A GPU reaches a container through the host driver, the NVIDIA Container Toolkit that injects device files and libraries, and the device plugin that advertises nvidia.com/gpu to the kubelet; the GPU Operator installs and manages all of them.

GPUs are integer extended resources set in limits; the scheduler counts them like CPU but cannot overcommit them, and node labels from GPU feature discovery plus taints direct GPU pods to the right nodes.

GPUs can be shared by time-slicing (no isolation), MPS (concurrent processes, limited isolation) or MIG (hardware partitions with isolated memory and compute), each exposed through the device plugin; Dynamic Resource Allocation adds claims with attribute selectors.
Distributed training needs gang scheduling so all pods of a job start together, and quota-aware queueing such as Kueue so teams share GPUs fairly without partial allocations deadlocking the cluster.

Cold start of a GPU replica is node provisioning plus image pull plus model download plus loading into GPU memory; with an 8.7 GB serving image and 16 GB of weights it is minutes on a cold node and seconds on a warm one.
Keep weights out of images: download to a node-local cache or shared volume, or mount them as an OCI image volume (stable since 1.36), and pre-pull serving images on GPU node images.
KServe's InferenceService runs models in Standard mode (Deployments with HPA or KEDA, recommended for LLMs) or Knative mode with concurrency-based autoscaling and scale-to-zero via an activator.
Autoscale inference on signals from the serving engine — waiting requests, in-flight requests, KV-cache usage — with long scale-down windows and warm capacity, rather than on GPU utilisation.
KubeRay runs Ray clusters as Kubernetes resources (RayCluster, RayJob, RayService), with Ray's autoscaler adding worker pods that node autoscalers then back with GPU nodes.
glossary: DCGM
NVIDIA Data Center GPU Manager: tooling and an exporter that report GPU health, utilisation, memory, temperature and errors.
device plugin
A node agent that advertises a hardware resource (such as nvidia.com/gpu) to the kubelet and tells the runtime which devices to give each container.
Dynamic Resource Allocation (DRA)
A Kubernetes API for requesting devices through ResourceClaims and DeviceClasses with attribute-based selection, allocated by the scheduler and prepared by drivers.
extended resource
A non-CPU, non-memory resource advertised by nodes, such as nvidia.com/gpu, requested in whole units in a container's limits.
gang scheduling
Admitting or starting all pods of a job together, or none, so partial allocations cannot hold resources while waiting.
GPU feature discovery (GFD)
A component that labels nodes with GPU properties such as product name, memory and count.
GPU Operator
An NVIDIA operator that installs and manages the GPU driver, container toolkit, device plugin, DCGM exporter, feature discovery and MIG manager on Kubernetes nodes.
image volume
A volume that mounts the contents of an OCI image or artefact read-only into a pod, useful for model weights; stable since Kubernetes 1.36.
InferenceService
KServe's custom resource describing a model server: model format and storage location, runtime, resources and autoscaling.
KubeRay
The operator that manages Ray clusters on Kubernetes through RayCluster, RayJob and RayService resources.
Kueue
A Kubernetes job-queueing system that holds jobs suspended until quota is available and admits them as a whole, with fair sharing between teams.
MIG (Multi-Instance GPU)
A feature of A100, H100 and later NVIDIA GPUs that partitions one GPU into up to seven isolated instances with their own memory and compute.
MPS (Multi-Process Service)
An NVIDIA feature that lets several processes run kernels on one GPU concurrently through a shared server, with limited isolation.
NVIDIA Container Toolkit
Host software that makes GPUs available inside containers by injecting device nodes, driver libraries and utilities.
scale-to-zero
Removing all replicas of an idle service and starting one again when a request arrives.
time-slicing
Sharing a GPU by interleaving processes over time, configured in the device plugin to advertise several virtual units per GPU.
XID error
An error code the NVIDIA driver logs for GPU faults (memory errors, fallen-off-the-bus, application faults), used by health checks.
drill:
Design: a GPU platform for a 40-person ML team

The team has 32 H100 GPUs (four 8-GPU nodes) on a managed Kubernetes cluster, plus the option of on-demand and spot GPU nodes from the cloud. Workloads: about ten notebooks, nightly fine-tuning jobs of 8-16 GPUs, and three production LLM endpoints (an 8B model with steady traffic, a 70B model with business-hours traffic, and an internal summariser used a few times a day). Today everything runs as plain Deployments and Jobs requesting whole GPUs; GPUs are 30% busy on average, the 70B endpoint breaches its p95 latency every morning, and fine-tuning jobs sometimes deadlock. Propose a design.

Answer

Nodes and sharing. Label and taint GPU node pools; install the GPU Operator. Partition one H100 node with MIG (for example 7 × 1g.10gb per GPU) for notebooks and the small summariser, which removes whole GPUs held by idle notebooks; cull idle notebooks after a few hours.

Training. Install Kueue with ClusterQueues per flavour (on-demand H100, spot H100) and LocalQueues per project; submit fine-tuning as suspended Jobs or JobSets so they are admitted whole (no more deadlocks); let them borrow idle inference capacity at night through a cohort, with preemption when serving needs it back; checkpoint every N steps to object storage so spot interruptions and preemptions cost minutes, not hours; annotate running jobs do-not-disrupt against consolidation.

Serving. KServe in Standard mode with vLLM. Scale the 8B and 70B endpoints with KEDA on num_requests_waiting per replica, long scale-down windows, and minimum replicas covering baseline; for the 70B endpoint, add a scheduled scale-up before the morning ramp and keep one warm GPU node via low-priority placeholder pods. Remove the cold-start path: weights as OCI artefacts mounted with image volumes or cached on node NVMe, serving images pre-pulled, startup probes sized to load time. Run the summariser in Knative mode with scale-to-zero on a MIG slice, accepting a cold start for occasional users.

Measure. GPU hours allocated versus busy per team, queue wait for training, cold-start time per endpoint, waiting requests and time to first token. Expected outcome: higher useful utilisation from MIG and borrowing, no gang deadlocks, and the 70B morning breach removed by pre-scaling and warm capacity rather than by permanently over-provisioning.
qa: E
How does a pod get a GPU in Kubernetes?

The node runs the NVIDIA driver, the container toolkit and the device plugin. The device plugin registers with the kubelet and advertises nvidia.com/gpu with the number of GPUs, which appears in the node's allocatable. A pod sets limits: nvidia.com/gpu: 1; the scheduler places it on a node with a free GPU; at container creation the kubelet asks the plugin to allocate a specific device, and the runtime injects that device and the driver libraries into the container.
E
Why can't you request 0.5 of a GPU?

Extended resources are integers and are not overcommitted: the scheduler hands out whole devices. Fractional use needs a sharing mechanism configured on the node: time-slicing or MPS, which make the device plugin advertise several units per GPU, or MIG, which exposes hardware partitions as their own resource names, or DRA with a driver that supports partitioning.
E
What is KServe?

A Kubernetes platform for model serving. You describe an InferenceService — model format, storage URI, runtime, resources — and KServe deploys the model server, wires routing and autoscaling, and supports canary rollouts. It runs in Standard mode as Deployments scaled by HPA or KEDA, which is recommended for LLM serving, or in Knative mode with request-concurrency autoscaling and scale-to-zero.
M
Compare time-slicing, MPS and MIG.

Time-slicing interleaves processes on the whole GPU over time: easy, works on any GPU, but no memory isolation or performance guarantees. MPS lets several processes' kernels run concurrently through a server process, improving utilisation for small workloads, with limited fault isolation. MIG partitions supported GPUs into up to seven instances with dedicated memory, cache and SMs: strong isolation and predictable performance, but fixed sizes and only on A100/H100-class hardware. Use MIG for multi-tenant inference, time-slicing for development and light jobs.
M
Why does distributed training need gang scheduling, and how do you get it?

A data-parallel job with 16 workers can only make progress when all 16 run. The default scheduler places pods individually, so two such jobs can each get part of their pods onto the free GPUs and wait forever for the rest, holding GPUs neither can use. Gang scheduling admits all of a job's pods or none: Kueue keeps the job suspended until its whole resource request fits within quota and then admits it, the coscheduling scheduler plugin uses PodGroups, and Volcano provides it natively.
Follow-up: What else matters for placement? — Topology: workers should share fast interconnects (NVLink within a node, the same network block across nodes), which needs topology-aware placement.
M
Estimate the cold start of a new LLM replica on a fresh GPU node.

Node provisioning and joining: one to three minutes, plus driver and toolkit readiness. Image: a vLLM serving image is about 8.7 GB compressed; at an effective 200 MB/s plus unpacking that is roughly a minute. Weights: an 8B-parameter model in BF16 is about 16 GB; at 1 GB/s from object storage, 16 seconds, at 200 MB/s, 80 seconds. Then loading to GPU memory and engine warm-up (graph capture, KV-cache allocation): tens of seconds. Total: three to six minutes cold, versus well under a minute on a warm node with image and weights cached.
M
Which metric would you use to autoscale an LLM inference service?

A signal from the serving engine that leads latency: the number of waiting requests per replica, in-flight requests, or KV-cache usage, exported to Prometheus and fed to an HPA through an adapter or KEDA. GPU utilisation is a poor signal because it measures the fraction of time a kernel is running, not how close the server is to saturation. Use a long scale-down window because new replicas are slow to start.
M
What does the GPU Operator install, and why use it?

The NVIDIA driver as a container, the container toolkit, the device plugin, GPU feature discovery for node labels, the DCGM exporter for metrics and health, and the MIG manager for partitioning, all as DaemonSets managed by one ClusterPolicy. It keeps driver and plugin versions consistent across nodes and upgrades them in a controlled way, instead of baking drivers into every node image by hand.
M
What is KubeRay and when would you use it?

KubeRay is an operator that runs Ray on Kubernetes. A RayCluster declares a head pod and worker groups (for example a GPU group); RayJob runs a job on a cluster and optionally tears it down; RayService runs Ray Serve applications with zero-downtime upgrades. Ray's autoscaler adds and removes worker pods, and the node autoscaler adds GPU nodes. Use it for Python-native distributed workloads — data processing, distributed training, hyperparameter search, multi-model serving — that are awkward to express as Kubernetes Jobs.
H
A training pod with 8 GPUs is OOMKilled during data loading although GPU memory is fine. What is happening?

The OOM kill is host memory, not GPU memory. PyTorch data-loader workers are separate processes, each with a copy of the dataset object and buffers; pinned host memory for transfers and shared-memory tensors passed through /dev/shm all count toward the container's memory limit (and a memory-backed emptyDir mounted at /dev/shm counts too). With 8 GPUs × 8 workers, that is 64 processes. Fix by sizing workers, streaming the dataset, sizing /dev/shm deliberately, raising the memory limit with request equal to limit, and reading memory.stat to see anon versus shmem.
H
Design a multi-tenant GPU platform for research training and production inference.

Separate node pools by GPU type, labelled by feature discovery and tainted. Production inference gets dedicated nodes with high priority, MIG partitions for small models, warm capacity, pre-pulled images and node-local model caches, served by KServe in Standard mode with KEDA on queue depth. Research training goes through Kueue: ClusterQueues per GPU flavour with quotas per team, cohorts so idle quota can be borrowed and reclaimed, gang admission, preemption of borrowed capacity, and checkpointing so preempted jobs resume. Observability from DCGM, Kueue and the serving engines; automated health checks cordon nodes with XID errors.

Follow-up: How do you stop research from starving production? — Different node pools and priorities: training can only borrow from research cohorts, and production pods have higher PriorityClasses on their own pools.
H
Why might an inference fleet's GPUs be 'fully utilised' yet latency is poor and adding replicas doesn't help?

Several possibilities: GPU utilisation is high because decode kernels run continuously, but the engine is limited by KV-cache memory, so requests queue (scale on queue depth instead); requests are pinned to a few replicas by long-lived connections or poor load balancing (use a request-aware router or Gateway inference extension); prefill of long prompts interferes with decode (chunked prefill, separate prefill and decode, lm13); or the bottleneck is CPU-side tokenisation or networking. Adding replicas helps only when the router spreads load and new replicas become ready quickly.
